# Pink Box — every record, flattened

## Dunkin' country (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/dunkin-country/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/dunkin-country.json
id: dunkin-country
aliases: New England coffee-and-donut · the regular
said: A regular means light and sweet, and you do not have to say so.
facets: state=MA · dough=both · counter=coffee-only
region: New England
what: Coffee first, donut second, at a counter that measures itself in how fast the line moves. The New England model, and the one the rest of the country meets as a drive-thru.
story: Bill Rosenberg opened the Open Kettle in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1948, selling donuts and coffee; in May 1950 he renamed it Dunkin' Donuts. He had been selling food to factories and construction sites and found donuts and coffee were what people bought. Franchising started in 1955. Johnny Spartos, running the original Quincy shop, talked Rosenberg into a donut with a handle, made for dunking.

The chain's growth came partly by absorption: in 1990 it took over Mister Donut — founded by Rosenberg's former partner Harry Winokur — and Dawn Donuts, converting the shops.

Density is the New England fact. The Providence metropolitan area has been cited as having the most donut shops per capita in the United States: 25.3 per 100,000 people, as of 13 January 2010.
how: Donuts arrive from a central kitchen in most locations now, which is the difference between this and a shop with a kettle.
today: A New England independent competes on frying on site and says so on the window.
- kin → dunkin (org): The company.
- kin → bill-rosenberg (person): Sold coffee to factories, then sold the idea.
- kin → allies-donuts (place): The Rhode Island counter that outlasted the argument.
- kin → donuts-per-capita (story): Where the shops actually are, counted.
sources: s:wp-dunkin-donuts — Dunkin' Donuts — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut-shop — Doughnut shop — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Fastnacht Day in the Dutch counties (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/pennsylvania-fastnacht/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/pennsylvania-fastnacht.json
id: pennsylvania-fastnacht
aliases: Pennsylvania Dutch fastnacht · Fasnacht Day
said: Pre-order by the dozen or do without.
facets: state=PA · dough=potato · counter=donuts-only
region: Pennsylvania Dutch country
what: One pastry, one day. Potato-dough donuts, square or diamond cut, fried for Shrove Tuesday and eaten with butter or golden syrup, sold by bakeries, churches, fire halls and — in eastern Pennsylvania — most chain supermarkets.
story: The fasnacht is a pantry-clearing food: lard, sugar, fat and butter used up before Lent. Lancaster, York, Lebanon and Berks counties keep it, and the day is known locally as Fastnacht Day rather than Shrove Tuesday. Parts of Maryland call them kinklings or kuechles, and bakeries there sell them only on that Tuesday.

Polish-American communities in the United States have largely moved pączki from the Thursday before to this same Tuesday, so in a city with both populations, one Tuesday carries two traditions and two arguments about which dough is better.
how: Potato dough, risen overnight, rolled, cut in squares with a slit, fried in the morning.
today: Volume is ordered ahead. A shop that guesses wrong on Fastnacht Day is wrong for a year.
- kin → fastnacht (donut): The donut itself.
- kin → fastnacht-day (event): The day.
- kin → paczki (donut): What the neighbours are frying the same morning.
- kin → spudnut (donut): The other American potato donut.
sources: s:wp-fasnacht-doughnut — Fasnacht (doughnut) — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The all-night counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/bay-area-late-counter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/bay-area-late-counter.json
id: bay-area-late-counter
aliases: 24-hour donut shop · the late window
said: Two in the morning is a different customer and the same donut.
facets: dough=both · counter=coffee-only · state=CA
region: The Bay Area, Southern California
what: A shop that never closes, or opens again at midnight: bar traffic, night shifts, students, and whoever else is out.
story: Bob's Donuts on Polk Street in San Francisco has run 24 hours and draws a nightlife crowd. Seaside Donuts Bakery in Newport Beach has been open around the clock since 1985. Randy's original drive-in in Inglewood is a 24-hour window.

The all-night shop is only possible because the fryer runs at night anyway — the overnight bake and the overnight trade are the same shift seen from two sides.
today: Where a city has a late counter, it tends to be one of the few places open at that hour that is not a bar or a hospital.
- kin → bobs-donuts (place): San Francisco's.
- kin → seaside-donuts (place): Orange County's.
- kin → randys-donuts (place): The Inglewood window.
- kin → the-2am-shift (kitchen): The shift underneath it.
sources: s:wp-bob-s-donuts — Bob's Donuts — Wikipedia; s:wp-seaside-donuts-bakery — Seaside Donuts Bakery — Wikipedia; s:wp-randy-s-donuts — Randy's Donuts — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The beignet stand (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/louisiana-beignet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/louisiana-beignet.json
id: louisiana-beignet
aliases: New Orleans beignet · the Quarter counter
said: Do not wear black, and do not inhale.
facets: state=LA · dough=choux · counter=coffee-only
region: Louisiana
what: An open-air or walk-up counter selling square fried dough under powdered sugar, three to an order, with coffee cut with chicory beside it.
story: French immigrants brought the pâte à choux method to New Orleans in the 1700s, and the square beignet is what it became there. Beignets are also made from yeast-leavened batters and from rice flour; the word covers all of them, and in Canadian French it simply means doughnut.

The coffee is the other half. The French brought coffee to the Gulf Coast around 1700, and Civil War shortages taught New Orleans to stretch it with chicory, which stayed after the shortage went.
how: Roll thin, cut squares, fry hot so they inflate hollow, sugar heavily while steaming, serve immediately.
today: Louisiana counters sell beignets, donuts and — in season — king cake off the same register, and nobody calls that a mixed menu.
- kin → beignet (donut): The item.
- kin → cafe-du-monde (place): The stand.
- kin → chicory-coffee (dish): What it is served with.
- kin → french-cruller (donut): The other choux fry in America.
sources: s:wp-beignet — Beignet — Wikipedia; s:wp-caf-du-monde — Café du Monde — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The Delta grocery counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/delta-grocery-counter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/delta-grocery-counter.json
id: delta-grocery-counter
aliases: Chinese grocery counter
said: The store came first; the fryer was added because the store was already open.
facets: dough=cake · counter=fried-rice
region: The Mississippi Delta, Chinese America, The American South
what: A small family grocery in the Mississippi or Arkansas Delta with a hot counter — and, in some of them, donuts fried in the morning beside the rest of the cooking.
story: Chinese labourers were recruited to the Delta by cotton planters during Reconstruction, most of them men from the Siyi region of Guangdong. By the end of the 1870s they had left the plantations and opened small family groceries in Delta towns, and families followed in the early 1900s. The stores served Black customers that white-owned stores treated badly, in a state whose records classified the owners as "colored".

*Inference —* the donut counter in a Delta grocery belongs to the same logic as the egg rolls in a California donut shop: a family business open early with a fryer already lit adds the thing that sells at that hour. This project has not found a published history of Delta grocery donut counters, and says so rather than inventing one.
how: Cake batter, a small kettle, and a case by the register.
today: The Delta Chinese community has thinned as generations left for cities; the stores that remain are fewer and older.
- kin → fried-rice (dish): What else is hot at the same counter.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): The same arithmetic, on a different river.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The easier dough for a counter that is not primarily a bakery.
sources: s:wp-chinese-americans-in-the-mississippi-delta — Chinese Americans in the Mississippi Delta — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## The hot light (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/southern-hot-now/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/southern-hot-now.json
id: southern-hot-now
aliases: Hot Now · the Southern glazed
said: The sign goes on and cars turn in. That is the whole marketing plan and it has worked since 1937.
facets: state=NC · dough=yeast · counter=donuts-only
region: The American South, The United States
what: A glazed raised ring handed over hot, minutes out of the fryer, with the glaze still moving. Built around a window you can watch the line through, and a lit sign that says the fryer is running.
story: Vernon Rudolph bought a yeast-raised recipe from a New Orleans chef, rented a building at 534 South Main Street in Winston-Salem in 1937 — now historic Old Salem — and sold to grocery stores. He also sold hot donuts to people who turned up during production, which ran from midnight to four in the morning. That is the origin of the whole idea: the hot donut was a by-product of the wholesale schedule, sold to whoever was awake.

The recipe traces back further, to Rudolph's uncle Ishmael Armstrong's general store in Paducah, Kentucky, and — by one account — to an Ohio River barge cook named Joseph LeBeouf, whose light doughnuts contained potatoes. The first store outside the South opened in Akron, Ohio, in 1939. A local architect, Benny Dinkins, drew the logo.

In the early 2010s the company began building shops with tunnel ovens so the hot sign could stay on all day, which is a different proposition from a sign that tells you the night shift is still going.
how: A continuous proofer and fryer in the window, a glaze waterfall at the end of the belt, and a warmer nobody pretends is the same thing.
today: Independent shops run the same trick without the sign: the raised dough comes out first, and the people who know arrive at opening.
- kin → krispy-kreme (org): The company that built the window.
- kin → hot-now (term): The two words as a term of art.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): The item.
- kin → the-2am-shift (kitchen): The schedule the hot donut fell out of.
- kin → vernon-rudolph (person): Bought the recipe, picked the town for a cigarette company.
sources: s:wp-krispy-kreme — Krispy Kreme — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The malasada counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/hawaii-malasada/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/hawaii-malasada.json
id: hawaii-malasada
aliases: Hawaiian donut shop
said: Sold hot, in a paper bag with sugar already in it.
facets: state=HI · dough=yeast · counter=donuts-only
region: Hawaii
what: A bakery counter in Hawaii selling malasadas — no hole, no filling by default, rolled in sugar — by the dozen in a box or hot by the piece in a bag.
story: Portuguese contract labourers from Madeira and the Azores brought the malasada to the islands. The pastry descends from filhós and was carried through Macaronesia by the sixteenth-century sugar trade. In Hawaii it stopped being a Carnival food and became an everyday one, which is not what happened to it anywhere else.

Malasadas are called Hawaiian donuts often enough on the mainland that the name has travelled back.
how: A wet, rich yeast dough, hand-pulled rather than cut, fried to order in the shops that can manage it, and dropped straight into sugar.
today: Filled versions — haupia, custard, guava — are standard now. The plain one is the one people queue for.
- kin → malasada (donut): The item.
- kin → leonards-bakery (place): The Honolulu bakery that made it a habit.
- kin → malasada-day (event): The day the lines get long.
- kin → mochi-donut (donut): The other Pacific arrival in the same case.
sources: s:wp-malassada — Malassada — Wikipedia; s:wp-leonard-s-bakery — Leonard's Bakery — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The mix-and-sign shop (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/tulsa-mix-shop/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/tulsa-mix-shop.json
id: tulsa-mix-shop
aliases: Daylight shop · franchise-flour independent
said: Same sign, same flour, different family, no head office telling them what to fry.
facets: dough=both · counter=kolaches
region: The United States, Texas, The American South
what: An independently owned shop trading under a shared name and buying its dry mix from one supplier. It looks like a chain from the road and is not one at the till.
story: Tommy and Lucille Day started in Tulsa in 1954, making donut mix in the mornings and selling it to shops in the afternoon, mostly out of the trunk of their car. The business they named was a flour company: Daylight Donuts Flour Co. The shops came after, and each Daylight Donuts store is independently owned and operated — roughly 950 of them, in 13 countries.

The Spudnut Shops ran the same way from 1940 with a dry potato mix, reaching more than 300 shops in 38 states by 1954 before the parent company disappeared and left the shops behind.

*Inference —* the mix is what makes a two-person shop possible: it takes the formulation off the owner and leaves them the frying.
how: Dry mix plus water, one kettle, one glaze table. The supplier's manual, not a corporate operations team.
today: Reading a sign as a chain misses who owns the shop. Reading it as a purely independent bakery misses whose flour it is.
- kin → daylight-donuts (org): The Tulsa flour company and its 950 signs.
- kin → spudnut (donut): The potato-mix franchise that went before it.
- kin → what-is-a-mom-and-pop (story): Where this project draws the line, and why it is blurry.
- kin → cake-batter (kitchen): What comes out of the bag.
sources: s:wp-daylight-donuts — Daylight Donuts — Wikipedia; s:wp-spudnut-shops — Spudnut Shops — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The New York corner counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/nyc-bodega-donut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/nyc-bodega-donut.json
id: nyc-bodega-donut
aliases: bodega donut · deli donut · Greek coffee shop donut
said: A coffee regular and a bacon egg and cheese on a roll, and the donut is an afterthought until it isn't.
facets: state=NY · dough=both · counter=bodega-sandwiches
region: New York City, Greek America
what: Donuts sold from a deli, bodega or coffee shop rather than a donut shop: a tray by the register, a grill behind the counter, and a bacon egg and cheese on a kaiser roll doing most of the business.
story: A bodega is a small owner-operated store selling hot and prepared food, often open late, defined by the city's health department as a store that sells milk, meat or eggs, is not a specialty store, and has no more than two registers. New York had an estimated 13,000 of them in 2020, and they are tied in the public mind to immigrant and Puerto Rican New York.

The bacon, egg and cheese is culturally particular to the city, where it comes on a kaiser roll. The donut arrives alongside it as the sweet half of the same transaction.

Greek immigrants ran a large share of the city's coffee shops and diners, and the Anthora cup — blue and white, Greek meander, "We Are Happy To Serve You" — was designed for exactly this trade.
how: Donuts are bought in, not fried on site, in most of these counters. The kitchen is a grill, not a kettle.
today: Dedicated donut shops in the city are a different business with different prices. The corner counter still moves more of them.
- kin → bacon-egg-and-cheese (dish): The sandwich that pays the rent.
- kin → anthora-cup (art): The cup the coffee comes in.
- kin → doughnut-plant (place): The other New York model: one shop, one obsession, higher price.
- kin → the-counter (story): What else is in the case, by region.
sources: s:wp-bodega — Bodega — Wikipedia; s:wp-bacon-egg-and-cheese-sandwich — Bacon, egg and cheese sandwich — Wikipedia; s:wp-greek-americans — Greek Americans — Wikipedia; s:wp-anthora — Anthora — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The novelty shop (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/novelty-donut-shop/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/novelty-donut-shop.json
id: novelty-donut-shop
aliases: concept donut shop · the topping arms race
said: Bacon on a maple bar was a joke once.
facets: dough=yeast · counter=donuts-only
region: The Pacific Northwest, The United States
what: A shop that competes on invention: unusual toppings, themed rooms, names that are jokes, and a queue that photographs its order.
story: Voodoo Doughnut opened in Portland in May 2003, night-only until 2006, with a logo carrying Baron Samedi. Psycho Donuts opened in Campbell, California in March 2009 with a straitjacket on the wall and donuts named after mental-health conditions, which has drawn objection. Doughnut Plant, from 1994, took the opposite route: invention aimed at pastry rather than at spectacle.

*Inference —* the novelty shop's real product is a photograph, which is why it prices above a strip-mall counter and why it ages faster.
today: The form spread nationally in the 2010s and the strip-mall shops largely ignored it.
- kin → voodoo-doughnut (place): The best-known one.
- kin → psycho-donuts (place): The most argued-over one.
- kin → doughnut-plant (place): Invention without the costume.
- kin → the-price-of-a-dozen (story): Where it sits on price.
sources: s:wp-voodoo-doughnut — Voodoo Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-psycho-donuts — Psycho Donuts — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut-plant — Doughnut Plant — Wikipedia

## The orchard window (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/new-england-cider/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/new-england-cider.json
id: new-england-cider
aliases: cider donut stand · farm stand donuts
said: Six for the car and six for the house, and the six for the house never arrive.
facets: dough=cake · counter=donuts-only
region: New England, Upstate New York
what: A seasonal counter at a cider mill, orchard or farm stand, running one machine and one product: cake donuts with cider in the batter, sugared and handed over hot in a paper bag.
story: Donuts belonged to autumn before anyone sold them at an orchard: the slaughter season produced the surplus fat you fried in. Cider donuts themselves go back at least to the late nineteenth century — a 1901 piece in The Buffalo Enquirer has them at Halloween parties.

What made them a roadside business was Adolph Levitt's 1921 machine, which fried rings of batter methodically and in public. Cider-selling farm stands took it up quickly. The Doughnut Corporation of America may have sold the first commercial cider donut, a "sweet cider doughnut", in 1951.

The season runs with the apples: September into November or December.
how: One depositor over one kettle, in view of the queue. Cider is reduced first, or the batter carries too much water. Donuts go into cinnamon sugar and then into a bag that goes translucent on the drive home.
today: Grocery stores start selling them in August and Dunkin' has run them as a seasonal item, which Food & Wine has pointed out is unlikely to involve fresh-pressed cider.
- kin → cider-donut (donut): The one product.
- kin → adolph-levitt (person): Whose machine made a farm stand into a donut shop.
- kin → orchard-season (event): The weeks it runs.
- kin → doughnut-corporation-of-america (org): Sold the first commercial version, and the machines.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The dough it belongs to.

## The Polish bakery counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/chicago-polish-bakery/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/chicago-polish-bakery.json
id: chicago-polish-bakery
aliases: paczki counter · Chicago Polish bakery
said: The line starts before the sun and the sign says how many you may buy.
facets: state=IL · dough=yeast · counter=donuts-only
region: Chicago, Detroit, The Upper Midwest
what: A Polish-American bakery selling pączki — rich filled donuts, powidła or rose-petal jam inside, powdered or glazed — beside rye bread and coffee cake. One day a year it is the only thing anyone is there for.
story: Pączki are medieval in Poland and were improved, Jędrzej Kitowicz wrote, by French cooks at the court of Augustus III until they came out lighter. The dough is richer than a jelly donut's — eggs, fat, sugar, yeast, sometimes milk — and carries a spoonful of rectified spirit, which evaporates in the fryer and keeps the oil out.

The pale belt around the middle is read as proof the oil was fresh. In Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit and Windsor the tradition sits with the Polish communities, and Fat Tuesday is Paczki Day.
how: Fresh oil, and the bakers say so. Fried in batches all night before the day, filled and sugared as they cool.
today: Hamtramck, Michigan, runs a Paczki Day the city closes streets for. Chicago bakeries post limits.
- kin → paczki (donut): The donut.
- kin → paczki-day (event): The Tuesday.
- kin → pennsylvania-fastnacht (style): The German-descended version of the same fast.
sources: s:wp-p-czki — Pączki — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-hamtramck-michigan — Hamtramck, Michigan — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The Southern California pink box (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/socal-pink-box/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/socal-pink-box.json
id: socal-pink-box
aliases: the pink box shop · SoCal independent donut shop · Cambodian-American donut shop
said: Nobody calls it a style. You say "the donut shop", and everyone knows which corner of which strip mall you mean.
facets: state=CA · dough=both · counter=egg-rolls
region: Southern California, Cambodian America, The United States
what: An independent counter, usually in a strip mall, usually open before five in the morning, frying both doughs in one small kitchen and selling them out of a matte pink box. Glazed raised, cake rings, buttermilk bars, fritters, bear claws, maple bars, holes in a bag. Coffee in a paper cup. Often, on the same board: egg rolls, croissant sandwiches, chow mein, boba, or a breakfast burrito.
story: Ted Ngoy left Cambodia with his wife and three children in 1975, ahead of the Khmer Rouge, and came through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program to Camp Pendleton. He took a janitor's job at a Lutheran church in Tustin and a second job at a gas station, noticed how busy a local donut shop was, and asked to learn the trade. An affirmative-action hiring program at the Winchell's chain trained him; he managed a store in Newport Beach and put his wife and nephew to work in it. In 1977 he bought his own shop, Christy's Donuts in La Habra, and named every shop he bought afterwards the same thing.

By 1979 he had more than 25 shops. He grew tired of running them himself, so he trained relatives and refugees and leased shops to them — "I sponsored more than 100 families", he said, and claimed each on official paperwork as kin. By 1987 he had 32 Christy's; at the peak he reckoned 65. The leasing model is the part that mattered: a family arrived, learned a trade in a month, took a shop, and a few years later sold or leased a shop to the next family.

KQED reported in 2021 that roughly 90 percent of California's 5,000-plus independent donut shops were Cambodian-owned. The pink box itself is attributed to Ngoy and Ning Yen, who were helping other Cambodians set up shops: cheaper matte pink stock instead of the glossy white box.

Why the second menu is there is not a mystery either. Jolly Chan, who opened China Express and Donut by the 24th Street BART station in San Francisco in 1993, put it plainly to KQED: "We have to sell more stuff to make up the rent and the expense."
how: One fryer, two doughs. Raised dough goes up overnight and is cut, proofed and fried first; cake batter is dropped from a depositor after. Glaze table by the door. Everything is done before the first commuter, and the case is not restocked — when the bars are gone they are gone. A second warmer holds whatever the shop also sells hot.
today: The model is under pressure from rents, from flour and shortening prices, and from the second generation going to college rather than to the bench at two in the morning. Shops still open, close and change hands quietly; the pink box outlives the owner's name on the sign. *Inference —* the box is the most portable piece of the whole thing, which is why it turns up in cities that never had the shops.
- kin → ted-ngoy (person): Trained at Winchell's, bought Christy's in La Habra, and leased shops to the families who followed.
- kin → ning-yen (person): Named with Ngoy as the reason the box is pink.
- kin → christys-donuts (place): The La Habra shop the whole pattern starts from.
- kin → pink-box (art): The object the style is named for here.
- kin → egg-roll (dish): On the board beside the glazed, and on it for a reason.
- kin → the-donut-king (story): The long version: refugee, empire, gambling, return.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): Rent arithmetic, told by the people who did it.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): The item the box is built around.
- kin → buttermilk-bar (donut): The tell of a shop that can run a cake bench.
- kin → randys-donuts (place): The one with the roof that everybody photographs.
- kin → winchells (org): Where the trade got taught, by a chain, to a refugee.
- kin → the-2am-shift (kitchen): When the work actually happens.

sources: s:wp-ted-ngoy — Ted Ngoy — Wikipedia; s:wp-cambodian-americans — Cambodian Americans — Wikipedia; s:kqed-donuts-chinese — Why Donuts + Chinese Food = A Very Californian Combination; s:wp-doughnut-shop — Doughnut shop — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The Southwest burrito counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/new-mexico-burrito-counter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/new-mexico-burrito-counter.json
id: new-mexico-burrito-counter
aliases: donuts and breakfast burritos
said: Red or green gets asked about the burrito, not the donut.
facets: state=NM · dough=both · counter=breakfast-burritos
region: New Mexico, The Southwest
what: A donut shop in New Mexico, Arizona or west Texas that also wraps breakfast burritos to order: scrambled egg, potato, cheese and chile in a flour tortilla, sold at the same window as the glazed.
story: The breakfast burrito is New Mexican before it is anything else. Tia Sophia's, a diner in Santa Fe, claims the first use of the term on a menu in 1975, though a tortilla rolled around eggs, bacon, potatoes and cheese was on New Mexican tables well before that. The fast-food chains followed — McDonald's in the late 1980s, Sonic, Hardee's and Carl's Jr. through the 1990s, Taco Bell in 2014.

The donut shop sits in the same slot as those chains: open early, one window, a driver in a truck. *Inference —* a counter already selling coffee at five in the morning has a griddle's worth of spare capacity and a customer who wants something salty, which is the same argument the California shops make about egg rolls.
how: A flat-top beside the fryer, a warmer of potatoes, a pot of chile. Burritos are wrapped in foil and stacked; donuts are boxed.
today: Where the burrito is on the board, it often outsells the donuts on a weekday morning. This project has not found a count that shows it.
- kin → breakfast-burrito (dish): The item itself.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The same second-menu logic, one state west.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): Why any of these counters sell something savoury at all.
- kin → the-counter (story): The map of what else is in the case.
sources: s:wp-breakfast-burrito — Breakfast burrito — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## The Texas kolache counter (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/style/texas-kolache-counter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/style/texas-kolache-counter.json
id: texas-kolache-counter
aliases: kolache shop · donut and kolache
said: Order a kolache in Texas and you will probably get sausage in it, which a Czech Texan will tell you is a klobasnek.
facets: state=TX · dough=both · counter=kolaches
region: Texas, Houston
what: A donut counter that also sells kolaches — and, in Texas, mostly klobasniky: sausage, ham, egg, cheese or jalapeño wrapped in sweet kolache dough. Sold from gas stations, strip-mall shops and dedicated kolache bakeries across the state, well outside the Czech settlement belt.
story: Two different pastries carry one name here. A traditional kolache came with Moravian immigrants: sweet dough with a fruit or cheese filling in a well on top. The klobasnek was invented by Czechs who had already settled in Texas — sausage wrapped in that same dough. Texans not of Czech descent call both kolaches; Texans of Czech descent call the savoury ones klobasniky and mean it.

The town of West, in McLennan County, has one of the largest concentrations of Czech Texans in the state and was designated "Home of the Official Kolache of the Texas Legislature" in 1997. Westfest keeps the day.

The donut shop picked it up because it sells at the same hour to the same driver. Fillings widened from klobása to hot dogs, ham and egg, cheese and peppers, and in some shops boudin, the Cajun pork-and-rice sausage.
how: Kolache dough is enriched and proofed like a sweet roll, wrapped around the sausage and baked, not fried — which means a Texas donut shop is running an oven as well as a kettle.
today: Kolaches travel where Texans travel. The word now shows up on donut counters in Oklahoma, Louisiana and Colorado, usually meaning the sausage kind.
- kin → kolache (dish): The sweet one, with the well and the fruit.
- kin → klobasnek (dish): The savoury one Texas calls a kolache.
- kin → czech-stop (place): The town the legislature named for it.
- kin → round-rock-donuts (place): A Texas counter big enough to be a landmark.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): The same arithmetic, a different second menu.
- kin → the-counter (story): What else is in the case, state by state.
sources: s:wp-klob-sn-k — Klobásník — Wikipedia; s:wp-west-texas — West, Texas — Wikipedia; s:wp-kolach-cake — Kolach (cake) — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Apple fritter (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/apple-fritter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/apple-fritter.json
id: apple-fritter
aliases: fritter
said: The heaviest thing in the case, and the one that sells out.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=glazed
region: The United States
what: Chopped apple and cinnamon folded through raised dough, torn rather than cut, fried craggy and glazed all over so the sugar catches in every fold. No two come out the same shape.
story: Fritter covers a wide family: a portion of batter or breading with a filling, fried. The word runs from the Latin frictura, frying, through the Old French friture. American shops use it for the apple one almost exclusively, and put the rest — corn fritters, clam fritters — in a different part of the food world entirely.
how: Fold diced apple through sheeted raised dough, cut and stack, press, then pull pieces apart so the edges stay ragged. Fry longer than a plain ring because the fruit carries water, and glaze heavy.
today: The fritter is the piece most often sold by weight in the shops that price by piece, because it is roughly two donuts of dough.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Same dough, torn instead of cut.
- kin → cider-donut (donut): The other apple one, cake, and seasonal.
- kin → bear-claw (donut): The other big ragged one, filled with almond instead of fruit.
- kin → glaze-table (kitchen): Glazed all over, not just the top.
sources: s:wp-fritter — Fritter — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Bavarian cream (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/bavarian-cream/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/bavarian-cream.json
id: bavarian-cream
aliases: custard-filled · cream-filled · Boston cream (when chocolate-topped)
said: Ask whether it is custard or whipped. The answer tells you what kind of shop you are in.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=filled
region: The United States
what: A raised round with no hole, filled with a set custard — Bavarian cream is custard lightened with whipped cream and held with gelatin — and finished in sugar, or iced with chocolate, at which point most counters call it a Boston cream.
story: The filled fried round is the older European form; the American shop split it by filling. Jam is a jelly donut or a bismarck; pastry cream and its relatives are custard, Bavarian or Boston cream depending on the shop and the region. The words are not standard and no authority governs them.
how: Fry the round, cool it, then inject from the side with a nozzle until it gains weight in the hand. Chocolate icing goes on the top face after.
today: The filled donuts are the ones a shop fills in the morning and the ones left over at closing, because a filled donut does not hold overnight the way a glazed ring does.
- kin → bismarck (donut): Same shell, jam instead of custard.
- kin → filling-injector (kitchen): The nozzle, and the weight in the hand.
- kin → long-john (donut): The bar version of the same filling.
- kin → day-old (term): What a filled donut is not sold as.

## Bear claw (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/bear-claw/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/bear-claw.json
id: bear-claw
aliases: bearclaw
said: Western word. Ask for one in Boston and you may get a look.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=iced
region: Southern California, Sacramento, The United States
what: A sweet yeast dough — bread dough carrying more shortening than usual — filled with almond paste and sometimes raisins, shaped in a semicircle with slices cut along the curved edge so the sections separate as it proofs, into toes.
story: The name is first attested on 13 March 1914, in a newspaper advertisement for the Geibel German Bakery in Sacramento, California. By the next year bear claws were on the breakfast menu at Hamburger's in Los Angeles, then the largest department store west of Chicago. The Sacramento Bee reports no earlier public reference; a Sacramento historian cautioned against crowning the city as the origin on that evidence alone.

The phrase is Western American English — the U.S. Regional Dialect Survey asks about it by name. Denmark calls the pastry a kam, Germany a Kamm; France has a patte d'ours, made in the Alps in 1982.

A bear claw cutter was patented into use in 1950 by James Fennell, which is when the shape stopped being purely a knife job.
how: Roll sweet dough around almond filling, cut four or five slits along one edge, curve it, proof it so the toes spread, bake or fry depending on the shop, then ice or glaze.
today: Donut shops sell it as a donut; bakeries sell the same thing as a Danish. Which one you get depends on which side of the counter it was made on.
- kin → apple-fritter (donut): The other big ragged piece in the case.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Sweeter, richer dough than the ring.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): A staple of the California case, and the name is a California word.
sources: s:wp-bear-claw — Bear claw — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Beignet (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/beignet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/beignet.json
id: beignet
aliases: French-style beignet · New Orleans beignet
said: Square, no hole, and the sugar is not optional.
facets: dough=choux · finish=powdered · state=LA
region: Louisiana
what: A deep-fried pastry of French origin, in New Orleans a square of dough fried until it puffs hollow and buried in confectioner's sugar. Beignet means bump.
story: The pâte à choux method — butter, eggs, milk or water, sugar, flour, salt, cooked and beaten — is the style French immigrants brought to New Orleans in the 1700s. Beignets are also made from yeast-leavened batters and from rice flour, and the word covers all of them. In Canadian French, beigne or beignet simply means doughnut. In the former French colonies of West Africa a beignet is a ball of fried dough, sometimes millet flour in Senegal.

The New Orleans beignet arrives at a table three to an order with a snowbank of powdered sugar and coffee cut with chicory beside it.
how: Roll the dough thin, cut squares, fry hot so they inflate and stay hollow, then sugar them heavily while they steam.
today: A donut shop in Louisiana may sell beignets, donuts and king cake off the same counter without anyone treating that as a mixed menu.
- kin → cafe-du-monde (place): The stand that made the square one famous.
- kin → louisiana-beignet (style): The style it anchors.
- kin → french-cruller (donut): The other American donut lifted by steam alone.
- kin → powdered-sugar (term): What it is buried in.

## Bismarck (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/bismarck/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/bismarck.json
id: bismarck
aliases: bismark · jelly donut · filled donut · Berliner
said: Upper Midwest word. Elsewhere you ask for a jelly.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=filled
region: The Upper Midwest, The United States
what: A round raised donut with no hole, fried, then injected with fruit preserve, custard or cream and finished in sugar or icing.
story: The filled fried dough is older than the ring by centuries. A recipe for Gefüllte Krapfen — stuffed fried dough cakes — is in Küchenmeisterei, printed in Nuremberg in 1485, and the form spread across Europe: the German Berliner, the Polish pączki, the Jewish sufganiyah, the Italian bombolone. In parts of Germany the same pastry is a Pfannkuchen, which means pancake everywhere else in the country and causes exactly the trouble you would expect.

Bismarcks and Berlin doughnuts turn up in Australia, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Switzerland and the United States. In the Upper Midwest the name stuck hard enough that a case label will say Bismarck and nothing else.
how: No hole: round the dough, proof it, fry it so a pale belt runs around the middle where it floated, then fill from the side and dust or ice.
today: A jelly donut is the one most likely to be filled to order in a shop that cares, and filled the night before everywhere else.
- kin → bavarian-cream (donut): Same shell, custard instead of jam.
- kin → paczki (donut): The Polish one, richer, and tied to a single Tuesday.
- kin → sufganiyah (donut): The Hanukkah one, fried in oil for the reason the holiday turns on.
- kin → filling-injector (kitchen): The nozzle that makes it what it is.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Same dough, hole instead of filling.
sources: s:wp-jelly-doughnut — Jelly doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-berliner-doughnut — Berliner (doughnut) — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:fdc-sr-legacy — FoodData Central, SR Legacy — doughnut foods
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Buttermilk bar (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/buttermilk-bar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/buttermilk-bar.json
id: buttermilk-bar
aliases: buttermilk donut
said: Split down the middle like it fell apart, which is how you know it is the right one.
facets: dough=cake · finish=glazed
region: Southern California, The United States
what: Cake batter cut in a bar rather than a ring, fried so it splits open along the top, and glazed heavily enough that the glaze runs into the split.
story: *Tradition holds —* the bar is a West Coast case staple and a test of a cake bench: too warm a batter and it will not crack, too cold and it breaks apart. It belongs to the same family as the old-fashioned, which cracks for the same reason, and shops that make a good one tend to make a good old-fashioned too.

No published history names an inventor or a first shop, and this project has not found one.
how: Buttermilk cake batter, rested cold, cut in rectangles, fried at a temperature low enough that the crust sets before the lift finishes. Glaze while warm.
today: Priced as a bar rather than a ring in most shops, which is to say a little more.
- kin → old-fashioned (donut): Cracks for the same reason, in a ring.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The batter it comes from.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): A fixture of the California dozen.
sources: s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: tradition · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Cake donut (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/cake-donut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/cake-donut.json
id: cake-donut
aliases: fry cake · cake-type · chemical-leavened donut
said: Some counters still call it a fry cake, and the older the sign, the likelier that is.
facets: dough=cake · finish=sugared
region: The United States
what: A ring of thick batter, not dough, raised by baking powder or soda rather than yeast and dropped straight into the fat from a depositor. It is denser, shorter and smaller than a raised ring — cake rings run 24 to 28 grams against the raised ring's 38 — and it takes sugar, cinnamon sugar or a heavy icing better than it takes a thin glaze.
story: The cake ring appears in American cookbooks in the 1830s, after pearlash — a potash refined for baking — became easy to buy, and it is the ring that industrialised. Yeast wants hours and a warm room; chemical leavening wants a mixer and a clock. When doughnut shops were streamlining production in the 1920s and 1930s, most bakers went the cake route because baking soda behaved the same way every morning and machines could be built around it.

The structural difference is in the flour as much as the lift: cake rings use cake flour, around 7 to 8 percent protein, which is why they crumb rather than pull.

The fat numbers depend on who you ask, and the two accounts do not agree. One puts cake at about 20 percent oil against yeast's 25; another puts cake at 20 to 25 percent and yeast at 25 to 35. Neither names a laboratory. What both agree on is the direction: the raised ring spends longer in the fat and comes out carrying more of it, and the cake ring makes up the difference with shortening mixed in before it ever gets there.
how: Beat a soft batter — cake flour, sugar, eggs, shortening, milk, baking powder. Rest it. Drop rings into 190 to 198 °C fat through a depositor, or cut them from a soft rolled dough. Fry roughly 90 seconds, turning once; one account has commercial cake rings out in 30 to 45 seconds at 191 °C. Sugar or ice them after they cool a little, because a hot cake ring drinks a thin glaze and goes soggy.
today: Cake is the dough that holds a flavour — buttermilk, sour cream, blueberry, chocolate, cider — so a shop that runs both doughs usually runs its specials on this side of the case.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): The other half of the argument: same fryer, different lift, different mouth.
- kin → old-fashioned (donut): The cracked, tapered cake ring people order by name.
- kin → cake-batter (kitchen): How it gets made, and why a machine could learn it.
- kin → cider-donut (donut): A cake ring with cider in the batter, sold by the bag at the orchard.
- kin → buttermilk-bar (donut): Cake batter cut in a bar, cracked open, glazed heavy.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): The argument, and what the numbers underneath it actually say.
- kin → fry-cake (term): What the older counters called it.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): Two doughs, two temperatures, one kettle.
sources: s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-old-fashioned-doughnut — Old-fashioned doughnut — Wikipedia; s:fdc-sr-legacy — FoodData Central, SR Legacy — doughnut foods
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Chocolate cake (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/chocolate-cake/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/chocolate-cake.json
id: chocolate-cake
aliases: devil's food · chocolate old-fashioned
said: Cocoa in the batter, not on the outside — the iced one is a different animal.
facets: dough=cake · finish=glazed
region: The United States
what: A cake ring with cocoa in the batter, glazed or sugared. Dark, dense, and sweeter than the plain cake ring on the published numbers.
story: Cake donuts hold a flavour the way raised dough does not, and chocolate is the oldest of the cake flavours in an American case. USDA publishes it as its own food — "Doughnuts, cake-type, chocolate, sugared or glazed" — separate from the chocolate-coated plain cake donut, which is a plain ring with icing on it and a different set of numbers.
how: Cocoa into a cake batter, dropped and fried like any cake ring, then glazed while warm.
today: The two chocolate donuts in a case — cocoa in the batter, or chocolate on the outside — get confused constantly, including by people selling them.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The family.
- kin → old-fashioned (donut): The plain cake ring beside it.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): Where its numbers sit.

## Cider donut (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/cider-donut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/cider-donut.json
id: cider-donut
aliases: apple cider doughnut
said: Bought hot at the mill, in a paper bag that goes translucent on the drive home.
facets: dough=cake · finish=sugared
region: New England, Upstate New York, The Upper Midwest
what: An American cake donut flavoured with apple cider, cinnamon and nutmeg in the batter, usually rolled in cinnamon or granulated sugar. Denser and moister than a plain cake ring because the cider is in the batter, not on it.
story: Cider donuts go back at least to the late nineteenth century — a 1901 piece in The Buffalo Enquirer has them at Halloween parties. Donuts had long belonged to autumn anyway: the slaughter season produced the surplus fat you fried them in.

The modern version follows the machine. Adolph Levitt's 1921 doughnut machine let anyone fry circles of batter methodically, and cider-selling farm stands took it up fast. The first commercially produced cider donut may have been the Doughnut Corporation of America's "sweet cider doughnut" in 1951.

Season runs with the apples: September through November or December. Grocery stores put them out as early as August, and Food & Wine has noted that a year-round cider donut is unlikely to have fresh-pressed cider in it.
how: Reduce cider, beat it into a cake batter with cinnamon and nutmeg, drop rings, fry, and roll in sugar while hot.
today: Sold at orchards, cider mills and farm stands as part of a day out, and by the half-dozen at the register of every farm store in the Northeast in October.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The dough it belongs to.
- kin → apple-fritter (donut): The year-round apple one, on the raised side.
- kin → orchard-season (event): The weeks it exists in.
- kin → new-england-cider (style): The style around it.
- kin → adolph-levitt (person): Whose machine let a farm stand fry.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/cider-donut/cider-donut-apple-cider-donuts-at-common-man-stop.jpg · CC BY 4.0 · Rjlevine · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AApple_Cider_Donuts_at_Common_Man_Stop.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/cider-donut/cider-donut-cider-doughnut.jpg · CC BY 4.0 · Rjlevine · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACider_Doughnut.jpg
sources: s:wp-cider-doughnut — Cider doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Donut holes (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/donut-holes/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/donut-holes.json
id: donut-holes
aliases: holes · munchkins · donut bites
said: A bag of holes is the only thing in the shop named after an absence.
facets: dough=both · finish=sugared
region: The United States
what: The centres cut out of ring donuts, fried and sold by the bag — or, more often now, made on purpose from the same dough or batter and never cut from anything.
story: When a cutter with two concentric circles came into use around 1870, every ring made a small disc of dough as a by-product. That disc could be fried and sold, or thrown back into the batch. The name sticks to the piece that was removed, not the space it left, which is why the thing you buy is the opposite of what you asked for.
how: Cut rings; collect the centres; fry them a shorter time than the rings, since they are smaller and rounder; roll in sugar or glaze in a tumbler.
today: Chains sell them as a named product in boxes by the dozen and half-dozen. Independent shops more often sell them by the bag, by weight or by scoop, and cheaper.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): The ring the hole came out of.
- kin → hole (term): The word, and the argument about who punched the first one.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): Cut the same way on the other side of the case.
sources: s:wp-donut-hole — Donut hole — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:fdc-sr-legacy — FoodData Central, SR Legacy — doughnut foods
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Fastnacht (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/fastnacht/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/fastnacht.json
id: fastnacht
aliases: fasnacht · faschnacht · fosnaught · kinkling
said: Spelled six ways in six counties, and everybody thinks theirs is the spelling.
facets: dough=potato · finish=sugared · state=PA
region: Pennsylvania Dutch country
what: A Pennsylvania Dutch fried donut, often made with potato dough, eaten in the days of Carnival and above all on Shrove Tuesday. Square or diamond cut, sometimes with a slit rather than a hole, sometimes plain, sometimes dusted with table sugar.
story: The point of it is the pantry. Fasnachts were made to use up lard, sugar, fat and butter before Lent, when households gave them up. The Pennsylvania Dutch counties — Lancaster, York, Lebanon, Berks and around — keep the day, and in eastern Pennsylvania the supermarkets carry them. Parts of Maryland call them kinklings or kuechles and bakeries sell them on Shrove Tuesday only.

The Polish pączek is the same idea a few hundred miles west. In Poland pączki are eaten on the Thursday before; in Polish-American communities the date has moved to Fasnacht Day, which is to say Tuesday.
how: Potato dough, risen, rolled, cut in squares or diamonds, slit in the middle, fried. Eaten with butter or golden syrup, which is the part outsiders find strange and Pennsylvania finds obvious.
today: Churches and fire halls still sell them by pre-order, by the dozen, and stop when the batch is gone.
- kin → fastnacht-day (event): The Tuesday it is for.
- kin → paczki (donut): The Polish one, richer, and on the same Tuesday in America.
- kin → spudnut (donut): The other potato donut, and a franchise built on it.
- kin → pennsylvania-fastnacht (style): The style around it.
sources: s:wp-fasnacht-doughnut — Fasnacht (doughnut) — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## French cruller (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/french-cruller/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/french-cruller.json
id: french-cruller
aliases: cruller · kruller
said: The light one. Ridged, hollow, gone in three bites.
facets: dough=choux · finish=glazed
region: The United States
what: A ring extruded from choux paste — flour cooked into butter and water, then beaten with eggs — piped through a star tip so it fries up ridged and hollow, and glazed thin. No yeast, no baking powder: steam lifts it.
story: Cruller is Dutch, from kruller, from krullen, to curl, and it arrives in America in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries with Pennsylvania Dutch settlers. In Europe the shape is a twist or a plaited rectangle pulled through itself; in North America the word covers both a small loaf- or stick-shaped cake doughnut and the French cruller, the choux ring. Milwaukee's cruller is the loaf kind: a glazed cake bar with a crunchy shell.

The word travels further than the pastry. Youtiao, the Chinese fried stick, gets called a Chinese cruller in English; so does mahua, the twisted one.
how: Cook the paste, beat in the eggs, pipe rings onto squares of paper, and slide them paper and all into the fat so they keep their shape. The paper lifts off once they set. Glaze while warm.
today: Few independent shops make them, because the paste is a different process from everything else on the bench, and the ones that do say so on the sign.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The other thing the word cruller covers in America.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Neither yeast nor powder — this one is lifted by steam alone.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): Piped onto paper, fried paper and all.
- kin → cruller-word (term): Dutch for curl, and what it came to mean here.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/french-cruller/french-cruller-french-crullers-in-a-doughnut-shop-display-case-in-c-0bbb8fe.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Jengod · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AFrench_crullers_in_a_doughnut_shop_display_case_in_California_2023_Jan_01.jpg
sources: s:wp-cruller — Cruller — Wikipedia; s:fdc-sr-legacy — FoodData Central, SR Legacy — doughnut foods
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Glazed raised (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/glazed-raised/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/glazed-raised.json
id: glazed-raised
aliases: raised glazed · yeast glazed · the glazed · plain glazed
said: Ask for a glazed and nobody asks which kind. It means this one.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=glazed
region: The United States
what: A ring of yeast dough, proofed until it is full of gas, fried about two and a half minutes, then dragged through a thin sugar glaze while it is still hot enough to melt it. The glaze sets into a shell you can hear. Yeast-raised rings run larger and taller than cake rings and average around 38 grams apiece.
story: The raised ring is the older idea and the harder one to run. Dutch settlers brought olykoek — oil cake — to New Amsterdam in the early eighteenth century, balls of sweetened dough fried in hog fat; Washington Irving put them in print in 1809 as "dough-nuts, or oly koeks". The hole arrives in the middle of the nineteenth century, credited by long habit to Hanson Gregory, a New England sailor who said he punched one out with a tin pepper box in 1847 at sixteen because the middles came out raw.

*Tradition holds —* that the hole was about heat reaching the centre. Culinary historian Linda Civitello writes that the hole made doughnuts cook faster; food writer Michael Krondl reckons the ring shape came off recipes that called for a jumble, a ring-shaped cookie already on the table. By 1870 a cutter with two concentric circles was on sale and the argument stopped mattering to anyone but historians.

When shops automated in the 1920s the raised dough lost ground: it needs time to rise and it is harder to handle, so machinery and baking soda pushed bakers toward cake. The raised ring survived because it is the one people mean.
how: Mix a lean, sweet dough with baker's yeast. Let it rise, sheet it, cut rings, then proof the cut rings again in a warm box until they are light enough to float. Fry about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C, turning once. Glaze hot: a thin syrup of powdered sugar and water or milk goes on within a minute of the fryer, so it soaks the crust and sets clear.
today: Every shop in the country sells it and most sell nothing else in that volume. A raised ring goes stale faster than a cake ring, which is why a shop that opened at four in the morning tells you so, and why the tray at noon is not the tray at six.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The other half of the argument: same fryer, different lift, different mouth.
- kin → yeast-raise (kitchen): What makes it rise, and the reason the shop was working at two in the morning.
- kin → glaze-table (kitchen): Where it gets the shell, seconds after it leaves the fat.
- kin → hole (term): The part that isn't there, and the part they sell you in a bag.
- kin → donut-holes (donut): The middles, fried and sold by the bag.
- kin → maple-bar (donut): The same dough, cut in a bar and iced instead of glazed.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The shop style that sells this one by the dozen before dawn.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): Why the two doughs split the case, and the numbers underneath.
- kin → hot-now (term): What a chain built out of glazing this exact donut in front of you.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/glazed-raised/glazed-raised-02023-0563-hot-doughnuts.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Silar · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3A02023_0563_Hot_doughnuts.jpg
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut-shop — Doughnut shop — Wikipedia; s:fdc-sr-legacy — FoodData Central, SR Legacy — doughnut foods
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Long John (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/long-john/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/long-john.json
id: long-john
aliases: bar · finger doughnut · cream stick · éclair (as sold)
said: Midwestern by default. In California the same thing is a bar.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=iced
region: The Upper Midwest, Texas, The United States
what: A bar-shaped raised donut, glazed all over or iced on top, sometimes filled with custard or cream.
story: Names for it are regional in a way few American foods still are. Long John dominates the Midwest, Canada and Texas. The Mid-Atlantic and central Canada market it as an éclair; the pastries look alike but an éclair is steam-puffed choux with fondant, and a Long John is yeast. The West Coast says bar. Parts of the Midwest say finger doughnut, or cream stick when it is filled.
how: Cut from sheeted raised dough into rectangles, proofed, fried, then glazed or iced. Filling goes in from the end with a nozzle.
today: A filled Long John is one of the few donuts a shop will cut open for you to prove what is inside.
- kin → maple-bar (donut): The West Coast name and the coast's favourite icing.
- kin → bismarck (donut): The other filled one, round instead of long.
- kin → bar-or-long-john (story): The map of what to call it.
- kin → filling-injector (kitchen): How the custard gets in.

## Malasada (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/malasada/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/malasada.json
id: malasada
aliases: malassada · Hawaiian donut · filhós (related)
said: No hole, no filling unless you ask, and sugar all over your shirt.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=sugared · state=HI
region: Hawaii, The United States
what: A flattened round of yeasted dough, fried and rolled in sugar — cinnamon sugar, often — with no hole and traditionally no filling. Portuguese from Madeira; Hawaiian by adoption, and the islands sell more of them than anywhere on the mainland.
story: The name is Portuguese: mal and assado, badly roasted, for the unstructured shape — or, another account has it, for the underdone dough inside. Malasadas descend from the mainland and Madeiran filhós, a product of the sixteenth-century sugar industry, and travelled through Macaronesia to the Azores, the Canaries and as far as Brazil. They are first described in the Dicionário Houaiss da Língua Portuguesa in 1609 and appear in the ledgers of the Convento da Encarnação in Lisbon between 1688 and 1762.

Portuguese contract labourers carried them to Hawaii, where they are called Hawaiian donuts often enough that the name has stuck to them in the rest of the country too. The Azorean malasada is a Carnival food; the Penedono filhós, made with brandy and olive oil instead of milk, is eaten year round, and the Portuguese agriculture directorate treats the two as distinct.
how: A rich yeast dough, rested, pulled into rounds by hand rather than cut, fried until it puffs, then dropped straight into a pan of granulated sugar.
today: Hawaii keeps a day for them. Shops sell them plain and filled — haupia, custard, guava — and the plain one is still the one that goes fastest.
- kin → leonards-bakery (place): The Honolulu bakery that made it a statewide habit.
- kin → hawaii-malasada (style): The island style around it.
- kin → malasada-day (event): The Tuesday it gets its own line out the door.
- kin → bismarck (donut): The other no-hole fried round, filled instead of sugared.
- kin → paczki (donut): Another Carnival donut that empties the pantry before a fast.

sources: s:wp-malassada — Malassada — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Maple bar (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/maple-bar/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/maple-bar.json
id: maple-bar
aliases: maple log · maple long john · maple creamstick · maple bismarck
said: On the West Coast it is a bar. Say Long John in Portland and you will be understood, and marked.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=iced
region: The Pacific Northwest, Southern California, The United States
what: A bar of raised dough, fried, then topped end to end with maple-flavoured icing. Sometimes filled with custard or cream; sometimes finished with chopped bacon, which is a newer idea and an argued one.
story: The same pastry carries different names by region. Long John runs through the Midwest, Canada and Texas; the Mid-Atlantic and central Canada sometimes sell it as an éclair, though an éclair is choux and this is yeast; parts of the Midwest say finger doughnut or cream stick when it is filled. On the West Coast it is a bar — maple bar, chocolate bar, filled bar — and the maple one is the one the coast is known for.
how: Sheet raised dough, cut rectangles, proof, fry, cool enough that icing will not run off, then dip the top face in maple icing and set it down icing-up.
today: A maple bar is the default second donut in a West Coast dozen — the one that goes in after the glazed.
- kin → long-john (donut): The same bar under the name most of the country uses.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Same dough, different cut and finish.
- kin → bar-or-long-john (story): Where the country changes the word.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): Two or three of these go in the box.

## Mochi donut (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/mochi-donut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/mochi-donut.json
id: mochi-donut
aliases: pon de ring · poi mochi
said: Eight balls in a ring, and you pull it apart rather than bite it.
facets: dough=other · finish=iced
region: Hawaii, Southern California, The United States
what: A chewy donut made with glutinous rice flour or tapioca flour, usually formed as a ring of eight connected balls that pull apart. Moist, springy, and heavier in the hand than it looks.
story: An early version traces to Hawaii in 1992, when Charmaine Ocasek made poi mochi — deep-fried balls of mashed taro and mochiko, Japanese sweet rice flour. In 2003 the Japanese chain Mister Donut launched pon de ring, named for the Brazilian cheese bread pão de queijo, and that eight-ball shape is the one that travelled: Japan, then Hawaii, then the mainland. Hawaii tends to pick up Japanese food before the rest of the country does.

Epicurious has pointed out the tangle in the name: neither pon de ring nor pão de queijo is typically made with glutinous rice flour — both lean on tapioca.
how: Rice or tapioca flour batter, piped as eight touching balls onto paper, fried, then iced in bright flavours.
today: Mochi donut counters opened across American cities through the 2020s, some as chains, some as a second case inside an older donut shop.
- kin → mochinut (org): The chain that put the shape in strip malls nationwide.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): Neither yeast nor powder; a third way of getting lift.
- kin → hawaii-malasada (style): The island case it shares.
sources: s:wp-mochi-donut — Mochi donut — Wikipedia; s:wp-mochinut — Mochinut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Old-fashioned (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/old-fashioned/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/old-fashioned.json
id: old-fashioned
aliases: old fashioned · sour cream old-fashioned · fry cake
said: The one that looks broken on purpose.
facets: dough=cake · finish=glazed
region: The United States
what: A cake ring with a cracked surface and tapered edges, glazed or sugared so the glaze pools in the cracks. The crack is the point: more surface, crisper edge, and a ring that holds up to coffee longer than a raised one.
story: The name has moved. Nineteenth-century cookbooks print old-fashioned doughnuts made with yeast; the old-fashioned in a shop case today is a cake ring raised with baking powder or soda, and has been described as a subset of the cake doughnut. Older counters called cake rings fry cakes, and the terms doughnut, cruller and fry cake have been argued over for as long as anyone has written them down.

Commercial versions often start from a dry batter mix that takes only water, which is one reason the same crack shows up in shops two thousand miles apart.
how: A stiff cake batter, chilled, cut thick. Into the fat cooler than a plain cake ring so the outside sets before the inside finishes lifting, which is what splits the surface. Glaze while warm.
today: Sour cream and buttermilk versions sell as their own items in most shops, and the plain glazed old-fashioned is the one that gets ordered with black coffee.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The family it belongs to.
- kin → buttermilk-bar (donut): Same batter, cut in a bar.
- kin → fry-cake (term): The older name for it.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): Cooler fat is what makes the crack.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): The argument this one anchors.
- kin → glaze-table (kitchen): Where the cracks fill.

## Pączki (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/paczki/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/paczki.json
id: paczki
aliases: paczki · punchki · pączek (sing.)
said: Pronounced closer to POONCH-key than anything the spelling suggests.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=filled
region: Chicago, Detroit, The Upper Midwest
what: A Polish filled donut: a flattened ball of rich dough — eggs, fat, sugar, yeast, sometimes milk — deep fried, filled with jam or cream, and finished in powdered sugar, icing, glaze or dried orange zest.
story: Pączki have been known in Poland since at least the Middle Ages. Jędrzej Kitowicz wrote that under Augustus III, French cooks in Poland improved the dough until pączki came out lighter and springier.

Two details separate them from a jelly donut. A small amount of grain alcohol — traditionally rectified spirit — goes into the dough; as it evaporates it keeps the oil from soaking in. And the bright pale stripe around the middle, from floating in fresh fat, is read as evidence the oil had not been used and reused.

Traditional fillings are powidła, stewed plum jam, and wild rose petal jam. American shops fill them with everything else as well.
how: Rich yeast dough with a spoonful of spirit, proofed, flattened, fried in fresh oil so the belt shows, filled from the side, sugared.
today: In Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee and Windsor the Tuesday before Lent runs on them. Lines start before dawn and bakeries sell by the dozen until the dough runs out.
- kin → paczki-day (event): The one Tuesday the whole thing turns on.
- kin → bismarck (donut): The German-descended cousin sold the rest of the year.
- kin → fastnacht (donut): The Pennsylvania Dutch answer to the same fast.
- kin → chicago-polish-bakery (style): The style it belongs to.
sources: s:wp-p-czki — Pączki — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Spudnut (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/spudnut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/spudnut.json
id: spudnut
aliases: potato donut
said: A word somebody trademarked, and the shops that still use it earned it.
facets: dough=potato · finish=glazed
region: Utah, The Mountain West, The United States
what: A donut made with potato flour or mashed potato in the dough. Softer crumb, longer shelf life, and a faint savoury note under the sugar.
story: Al and Bob Pelton of Salt Lake City ate potato doughnuts in Germany, then worked through wheat dough flavoured with potato water and mashed potato before landing on a dry potato mix that could be shipped — which is what made a franchise possible. They coined the word spudnut and opened in 1940.

The chain moved fast. Franchising began in 1946; in 1948 a new franchisee paid fifty dollars plus the cost of a hundred sacks of spudnut flour; by mid-1949 there were more than 225 shops in 31 states, more than 300 in 38 states by 1954, and 315 by 1968. The advertising ran "Coast to coast… Alaska to Mexico", with a cartoon Mr. Spudnut in parades.

The parent company is gone. Independent shops still trading under the name are the survivors of that system, not a chain.
how: Potato flour or riced potato into a yeast dough, proofed, cut and fried like any raised ring.
today: A Spudnut sign is a dated object: it marks a shop that bought into a franchise that no longer exists and kept the name.
- kin → fastnacht (donut): The other American potato donut, and older.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What it is, under the potato.
- kin → the-franchise-that-vanished (story): How a 300-shop system leaves independent shops behind.
- kin → neon-donut (art): Spudnut signs are half the reason those signs get photographed.
sources: s:wp-spudnut-shops — Spudnut Shops — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Sufganiyah (donut)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/donut/sufganiyah/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/donut/sufganiyah.json
id: sufganiyah
aliases: sufganiyot · Hanukkah donut
said: Fried in oil, for a reason the holiday turns on.
facets: dough=yeast · finish=filled
region: New York City, The United States
what: A round filled donut, traditionally red jelly with icing sugar on top, eaten at Hanukkah. Dulce de leche fillings became common after South American immigration to Israel early in this century.
story: Jelly or custard-filled donuts are a Hanukkah tradition because they are cooked in oil, which is the miracle the holiday commemorates: one day's oil kept the Temple menorah burning for eight. The sufganiyah belongs to the same European family as the Berliner, the pączek and the bombolone, whose common ancestor is the Gefüllte Krapfen of a 1485 Nuremberg cookbook.
how: Rich yeast dough, rounded and proofed, fried, filled from the side, dusted.
today: American bakeries and donut shops in Jewish neighbourhoods run them for the eight days and mark them on the board by name.
- kin → bismarck (donut): The same round under a different name.
- kin → paczki (donut): Another calendar donut, another fast.
- kin → filling-injector (kitchen): How it is filled.

said: On a roll, salt pepper ketchup, and the order is said as one word.
facets: course=breakfast · state=NY
region: New York City
what: Bacon, fried or scrambled egg and cheese on bread — in New York City, on a kaiser roll. About 20 grams of fat and 350 calories in a typical one.
story: The sandwich is common across the United States and Canada and culturally particular to New York, where the deli, the bodega and the corner coffee shop all make it to order and wrap it in foil and paper. It is abbreviated BEC in print and said as a single word at the counter.
today: Where the sandwich is the business, the donut is the impulse buy beside the register rather than the reason anyone came in.

said: The newest thing on an old board, usually in a different typeface.

what: Tea with milk and tapioca pearls, sealed under a film lid and drunk through a fat straw.
story: Bubble tea came out of Taiwan in the 1980s and spread through Taiwanese and Chinese diaspora communities. American donut shops with Asian-American owners have added it to the board as a second-generation move: a product with a young customer and a better margin than a glazed.
today: A shop that adds boba is usually adding it beside the donuts, not instead of them.

## Breakfast burrito (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/breakfast-burrito/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/breakfast-burrito.json
id: breakfast-burrito
aliases: breakfast wrap
said: Foil-wrapped, eaten one-handed, and the chile question comes with it.
facets: course=breakfast
region: New Mexico, The Southwest
what: Breakfast inside a flour tortilla: scrambled egg, potato, cheese, and in the Southwest, New Mexico chile, jalapeño, salsa, onion, chorizo or bacon.
story: It comes out of New Mexican cooking. Tia Sophia's, a diner in Santa Fe, claims the first use of the term on a menu in 1975, though a tortilla rolled around eggs, bacon, potatoes and cheese predates the name. McDonald's added a version in the late 1980s; Sonic, Hardee's and Carl's Jr. followed in the 1990s; Taco Bell in 2014. Dunkin' sells one too.
today: A donut shop with a griddle sells them to the same driver at the same hour, which is the whole reason they share a board.
