## Coffee with chicory (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/chicory-coffee/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/chicory-coffee.json
id: chicory-coffee
aliases: café au lait · New Orleans coffee
said: Half coffee, half hot milk, and the chicory is not optional.
facets: course=drink · state=LA
region: Louisiana
what: Coffee blended with roasted chicory root and cut half-and-half with hot milk.
story: The French brought coffee to the Gulf Coast and the Mississippi around 1700. During the Civil War, with coffee short, New Orleans Creoles stretched it with chicory, which adds a chocolate-like note. The practice outlived the shortage.
today: Served at Café du Monde and across New Orleans, beside beignets, in a cup that leaves sugar on the rim.
- kin → cafe-du-monde (place): Where most people meet it.
- kin → beignet (donut): What it is served with.
- kin → the-pot-of-coffee (dish): What the rest of the country pours instead.
sources: s:wp-caf-du-monde — Café du Monde — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Egg roll (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/egg-roll/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/egg-roll.json
id: egg-roll
aliases: eggroll
said: Two for a dollar something, in the warmer by the register, and nobody explains why.
facets: course=savory
region: Southern California, Chinese America, The United States
what: A cylindrical deep-fried roll in a thick wheat skin — shredded cabbage, chopped meat, sometimes shrimp — eaten with the fingers out of a cellophane packet of duck sauce. Despite the name it generally has no egg in it, though egg white sometimes seals the seam.
story: The egg roll is American. It is distinct from mainland Chinese spring rolls and first appears in the United States in the early twentieth century. Andrew Coe, who wrote Chop Suey: A Cultural History of Chinese Food in the United States, reckons the modern American egg roll was probably invented at a New York Chinese restaurant in the early 1930s by one of two chefs who each later claimed it: Lung Fong of Lung Fong's, or Henry Low of Port Arthur. Low's recipe, printed in the 1938 cookbook Cook at Home in Chinese, called for bamboo shoots, roast pork, shrimp, scallions, water chestnuts, salt, MSG, sugar, palm oil and pepper.

Why it is in a donut shop is a separate question with a plain answer: rent. Jolly Chan, who runs China Express and Donut in San Francisco, told KQED the combination "came out of necessity" — "we have to sell more stuff to make up the rent and the expense."
today: In Southern California a hot case beside the donuts holds egg rolls, and often chow mein and fried rice with them. The fryer was already on.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The shop it shares a fryer with.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): The whole argument, told by the people running the shops.
- kin → fried-rice (dish): What sits next to it in the warmer.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): One kettle, two menus.
sources: s:wp-egg-roll — Egg roll — Wikipedia; s:kqed-donuts-chinese — Why Donuts + Chinese Food = A Very Californian Combination
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Fried rice and chow mein (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/fried-rice/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/fried-rice.json
id: fried-rice
aliases: chow mein · the hot case
said: Kept in a warmer, sold by the scoop, priced under the sandwich.
facets: course=savory
region: Southern California, Chinese America
what: Cooked rice stir-fried with egg, vegetables and meat, held hot in a steam table beside the donut case — with chow mein next to it in many shops.
story: Fried rice is a staple of Chinese cooking and of American Chinese menus. In California donut shops it arrives for the same reason egg rolls do: the shop needs a second product at a second hour, and the kitchen can already do it.

Dorothy Chow's family business, B & H Bakery Distributors, supplies these shops; her father, a survivor of the Cambodian genocide, built it, she told KQED, "to help our own people."
today: A donut shop with a steam table is doing lunch, which is a different business from the one it does at five in the morning.
- kin → egg-roll (dish): The other thing in the warmer.
- kin → delta-grocery-counter (style): The same counter logic in Mississippi.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): The argument.

## Klobasnek (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/klobasnek/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/klobasnek.json
id: klobasnek
aliases: klobásník · klobasniky · Texas kolache (as sold)
said: Ask a Czech Texan and you get the distinction; ask anyone else and you get a sausage roll.
facets: course=savory · state=TX
region: Texas, Houston
what: Sausage — klobása, traditionally — wrapped in kolache dough and baked. Ham, egg, cheese, jalapeño and hot dog are all standard now, and in some Texas shops boudin, the Cajun pork-and-rice sausage.
story: Unlike the kolache, which came with Moravian immigrants, the klobasnek was invented by Czechs who had already settled in Texas. Texans of Czech ancestry call the savoury doughs klobasniky; Texans who are not call them kolaches, and that is what the sign says. They are sold everywhere from gas stations to dedicated kolache shops, well outside the Czech counties.
today: The klobasnek is the reason a Texas donut shop runs an oven.
- kin → kolache (dish): The sweet one whose name it borrowed.
- kin → texas-kolache-counter (style): The counter it built.
- kin → czech-stop (place): The stop on I-35 that sells them around the clock.
sources: s:wp-klob-sn-k — Klobásník — Wikipedia

## Kolache (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/kolache/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/kolache.json
id: kolache
aliases: koláč · kolach · kolaches
said: "Kolaches" is a double plural and Texas says it anyway.
facets: course=sweet · state=TX
region: Texas
what: A sweet bread with a well of fruit or cheese in the middle of puffy yeast dough — tvaroh, jam, poppy seed, or povidla, which is prune. Baked, not fried.
story: The word comes from Czech and Slovak koláč, from the Old Slavonic kolo, a circle or wheel. Traditional Czech koláče are small, no more than about eight centimetres across, and are village feast and wedding food. Moravian immigrants brought them to the United States.

In American English kolache is often used as the singular and given an extra s, which makes kolaches a double plural. Czech Texans notice.
today: Texas donut counters sell them beside the savoury ones, and the savoury ones outsell them.
- kin → klobasnek (dish): The savoury one Texas calls by this name.
- kin → texas-kolache-counter (style): The counter style.
- kin → czech-stop (place): The town the legislature named for it.

## The pot of coffee (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/dish/the-pot-of-coffee/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/dish/the-pot-of-coffee.json
id: the-pot-of-coffee
aliases: drip coffee · the regular · bottomless cup
said: Refills happen without the question being asked, which is most of the reason people sit down.
facets: course=drink
region: The United States
what: Drip coffee from a glass pot on a warmer, in a paper cup or a mug, refilled by whoever is at the counter.
story: Coffee and donuts were paired commercially before either was a chain: Bill Rosenberg's finding, selling food to factories and construction sites in the 1940s, was that donuts and coffee were the two items people bought. He built a company on the pair. The dunking that gave Dunkin' its name was ordinary behaviour first; Johnny Spartos, running the Quincy shop, talked Rosenberg into making a donut with a handle for it.
today: An independent shop's coffee is rarely the reason to go, and a shop that raises the coffee price before the donut price is telling you where its margin is. *Inference —* that reading is this project's, not a published finding.
- kin → dunkin-country (style): The chain that paired them nationally.
- kin → bill-rosenberg (person): Found the pairing selling to factories.
- kin → chicory-coffee (dish): The New Orleans version.

## Cutting by hand (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/hand-cut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/hand-cut.json
id: hand-cut
aliases: the bench · hand-cut · the cutter
said: A shop that says hand-cut on the window is drawing a line, and everyone in the trade knows which one.
facets: kind=cut
region: The United States
what: Rolling sheeted dough and cutting rings with a two-ring cutter, rather than depositing or buying pre-formed shells.
story: Cutters with two concentric circles were on sale by 1870, which is when the ring and its hole became a manufactured thing rather than a trick with a pepper box. A ring can also be made by joining the ends of a rope of dough, or by stretching a disc until the middle tears.
how: Sheet, cut in rows, lift the rings onto screens, gather and re-roll the scrap once — twice makes it tough.
today: Hand-cut is a claim a shop makes on its sign. This project records the claim and its source, and does not test it.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What the bench is for.
- kin → allies-donuts (place): A shop that put the words in its name.
- kin → donut-holes (donut): What the small ring leaves behind.

## Day-old (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/day-old-rack/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/day-old-rack.json
id: day-old-rack
aliases: the day-old rack · yesterday's
said: Half price, in a bag, and the sign does not apologise.
facets: kind=hold
region: The United States
what: Yesterday's donuts, sold cheap the next morning, usually bagged rather than boxed and usually the rings rather than the filled ones.
story: *Tradition holds —* the rack exists because a donut's shelf life is one morning and a shop's costs are not. Raised rings go stale fastest; cake rings hold longer, which is part of why the cake side of the case is the one that turns up marked down.

This project has found no published study of American day-old donut pricing, and says so rather than estimating one.
how: Bag what is left at close, price it at open.
today: Where a shop puts the day-old rack — by the till or out of sight — says how it would like to be thought of.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Stales first.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): Holds longer.
- kin → day-old (term): The word.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: tradition · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Dipping and sprinkles (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/sprinkle-and-dip/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/sprinkle-and-dip.json
id: sprinkle-and-dip
aliases: jimmies · nonpareils · the dip
said: New England says jimmies. Almost nowhere else does.
facets: kind=finish
region: The United States
what: Icing in flat pans, sprinkles in bins: a donut is dipped face-down, then set in the sprinkles while the icing is still wet.
story: Sprinkles are small pieces of confectionery used as decoration. The long ones are called jimmies in parts of the United States, above all New England and Philadelphia; the tiny balls are nonpareils. Chocolate, maple, strawberry and vanilla icings are the standard dips, and the colour on a shop's sprinkles is one of the few things it chooses purely to look like itself.
how: Dip, lift, tilt to shed the excess, then straight into the tray of sprinkles before it sets.
today: A case of sprinkled donuts is the shop's shop window, which is why the bright ones sit at eye level.
- kin → glaze-table (kitchen): What happens first.
- kin → the-case (kitchen): How the tray is laid out.
- kin → jimmies (term): The word, and where it stops.

## The batter and the depositor (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/cake-batter/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/cake-batter.json
id: cake-batter
aliases: depositor · the drop
said: Two levers and a plunger: the ring lands in the fat already round.
facets: kind=mix
region: The United States
what: A thick chemically-leavened batter dropped straight into hot fat through a hand-held or bench depositor, which forms the ring as it falls.
story: Cake batter uses cake flour, about 7 to 8 percent protein, and baking powder or soda rather than yeast. Commercial shops often start from a dry mix that takes only water — which is how the same donut turns up in shops two thousand miles apart.

This is the dough that industrialised. When shops were streamlining in the 1920s and 1930s, chemical leavening behaved the same way every morning and a machine could be built around it.
how: Mix, rest, load the hopper, drop rings in rows, and turn them once with sticks when the underside sets.
today: A depositor is what lets one person run a case alone.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): What comes out of it.
- kin → yeast-raise (kitchen): The slower way.
- kin → tulsa-mix-shop (style): The shops that buy the mix rather than the formula.
- kin → adolph-levitt (person): Whose machine started the idea.
sources: s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut-shop — Doughnut shop — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The case (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/the-case/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/the-case.json
id: the-case
aliases: the display · the tray
said: Top shelf is what the shop wants you to see. Bottom shelf is what it has a lot of.
facets: kind=hold
region: The United States
what: The glass case: trays by kind, tongs on a hook, and a layout that repeats across the country without anyone having agreed on it.
story: *Inference —* the arrangement follows the frying order more than any merchandising plan. Raised glazed comes out first and takes the biggest tray; cake and old-fashioned follow; filled and iced pieces, which are finished last, land at the front where they look best and sell first.
how: Load hot, front the trays as they empty, and stop refilling a few hours before close.
today: A case that is still full at ten in the morning is a shop that made too many, and a case that is empty at eight is a shop that could have sold more. Neither is visible from the road.
- kin → sprinkle-and-dip (kitchen): What makes the front row bright.
- kin → day-old-rack (kitchen): Where the leftovers go.
- kin → the-dozen (term): How it gets sold.

## The filler (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/filling-injector/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/filling-injector.json
id: filling-injector
aliases: the injector · the nozzle · the pump
said: You can hear a filled donut being made: a thump and a hiss, once per piece.
facets: kind=finish
region: The United States
what: A hand pump or bench machine that pushes jam, custard or cream through a nozzle into the side of a fried round.
story: Filled fried dough is older than the ring — Gefüllte Krapfen are in a Nuremberg cookbook of 1485 — but the injector is what makes a case full of them possible before six in the morning. Fillings run to fruit preserve, custard, Bavarian cream, and in Polish shops powidła, stewed plum, and wild rose petal jam.
how: Fry, cool, weigh the first few to set the dose, then work a tray at a time.
today: A filled donut does not hold overnight the way a glazed ring does, which is why it is the one most often made last and sold out first.
- kin → bismarck (donut): The round it fills.
- kin → bavarian-cream (donut): The custard version.
- kin → paczki (donut): Powidła and rose petal.
- kin → day-old (term): What filled donuts are not sold as.

## The glaze table (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/glaze-table/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/glaze-table.json
id: glaze-table
aliases: the waterfall · the dip
said: Glaze goes on hot or it goes on wrong.
facets: kind=finish
region: The United States
what: A shallow pan of thin sugar glaze beside the fryer, where raised rings are dragged through face-down within a minute of coming out of the fat.
story: Glaze is a thin coating applied to food — here, powdered sugar with water or milk and sometimes a little fat, thin enough to run off and set clear. On a hot ring it soaks the crust and hardens into a shell; on a cool one it sits on top and stays tacky.

Cake rings are finished differently for the same reason: a hot cake ring drinks a thin glaze and goes soggy, so it takes sugar, cinnamon sugar or a heavier icing instead.
how: Dip, turn, lift, drain on a screen. The pan is topped up all morning and the glaze thickens as the shop warms.
today: The glaze table is where a shop's whole tray of raised donuts is either made or ruined, in about a minute each.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What goes across it.
- kin → powdered-sugar (term): What it is made of.
- kin → sprinkle-and-dip (kitchen): What happens after.
- kin → southern-hot-now (style): A chain that put the table in the window.
sources: s:wp-glaze-cooking — Glaze (cooking) — Wikipedia; s:wp-powdered-sugar — Powdered sugar — Wikipedia; s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The kettle (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/the-fryer/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/the-fryer.json
id: the-fryer
aliases: the fryer · the vat · the flip
said: One kettle, two temperatures, and a pair of sticks.
facets: kind=fry
region: The United States
what: A shallow open kettle of hot fat with a screen, where every donut in the shop is cooked, turned once, and lifted out.
story: The two doughs want different heat. Yeast-raised rings fry about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C and absorb more fat for it — around 25 percent by weight. Cake rings fry about 90 seconds at 190 to 198 °C, turning once, and run near 20 percent, with extra shortening already in the batter.

The numbers are not settled. Another account puts cake at 20 to 25 percent and yeast at 25 to 35, and commercial cake rings at 30 to 45 seconds at 191 °C. Neither cites a laboratory, and this project reports both rather than picking.
how: Drop, wait for the belt to show, flip with sticks, wait, lift onto the drain screen.
today: Every other decision in the shop is downstream of how many rings fit on the surface of the fat at once.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): Longer in the fat, and carries more of it.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): Shorter, hotter, and drier out of the kettle.
- kin → frying-fat (kitchen): What is in the kettle.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): The numbers, side by side.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-deep-frying — Deep frying — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The night shift (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/the-2am-shift/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/the-2am-shift.json
id: the-2am-shift
aliases: the two o'clock · the night bake
said: The light is on and the door is locked, and that is the shop working.
facets: kind=shift
region: The United States
what: The hours the work actually happens in: dough started in the small hours so the case is full when the door opens.
story: Krispy Kreme's hot donut began as a by-product of exactly this. Vernon Rudolph's Winston-Salem shop sold wholesale to grocery stores, and production ran from midnight to four in the morning; he sold hot donuts to whoever turned up during it. The window came later; the schedule came first.

A raised dough sets the clock. It has to be mixed, risen, cut, proofed and fried before opening, and none of those steps can be hurried by much.
how: Mix around midnight or one. Raised first, cake after. Glaze, ice, fill, sprinkle, load the case, unlock the door.
today: The shift is the part of the business that does not scale, and the part a family absorbs. *Inference —* it is also the reason a second generation often does not take the shop on.
- kin → yeast-raise (kitchen): What sets the clock.
- kin → southern-hot-now (style): The chain that sold the by-product.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): Whose families work it.
- kin → vernon-rudolph (person): Sold hot donuts to the people awake at 2 a.m.
sources: s:wp-krispy-kreme — Krispy Kreme — Wikipedia; s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The proof box (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/proof-box/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/proof-box.json
id: proof-box
aliases: proofer · the cabinet
said: Warm, damp, and the one thing in the shop nobody opens without a reason.
facets: kind=raise
region: The United States
what: A warm humid cabinet where cut rings take their final rise before they go in the fat.
story: *Tradition holds —* a proof box is run warm and wet so the skin does not dry: a dried skin will not expand and the ring fries lopsided. Shops without a box use a rack near the fryer and the room's own heat, which is why a raised dough behaves differently in January.
how: Rings go in on screens, come out when they wobble.
today: The box is the piece of equipment that decides whether a shop can run raised dough at volume.
- kin → yeast-raise (kitchen): The process it serves.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What is in there.
sources: s:wp-proofing-baking-technique — Proofing (baking technique) — Wikipedia
provenance default: tradition · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The raise (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/yeast-raise/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/yeast-raise.json
id: yeast-raise
aliases: proofing · the rise · bulk ferment
said: The dough is worked when it is ready, not when the clock says.
facets: kind=raise
region: The United States
what: Baker's yeast fermenting a sweet dough until it is full of gas — once in bulk, once again after the rings are cut.
story: Proofing is the rest in which yeast ferments the dough and makes the gas that lifts it. Blooming is a different thing with the same word: suspending dry yeast in warm water to hydrate it, and to see whether it is still alive.

The raise is why the raised donut lost ground when shops automated in the 1920s. Yeast needs time and a warm room, and the dough is harder to handle; baking soda was predictable and easy to build a machine around, so most bakers went to cake.
how: Mix, bulk rise, sheet, cut, then proof the cut rings again in a warm cabinet until they are light enough to float sideways in the fat.
today: The raise is the reason the shop opens at four and the work started at one.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What comes out of it.
- kin → proof-box (kitchen): Where the second rise happens.
- kin → cake-batter (kitchen): The other way to get lift, and the one machines preferred.
- kin → the-2am-shift (kitchen): What the raise does to the schedule.
sources: s:wp-proofing-baking-technique — Proofing (baking technique) — Wikipedia; s:wp-baker-s-yeast — Baker's yeast — Wikipedia; s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## What is in the kettle (kitchen)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/kitchen/frying-fat/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/kitchen/frying-fat.json
id: frying-fat
aliases: shortening · lard · frying oil
said: Ask what they fry in and you learn how old the shop is.
facets: kind=fry
region: The United States
what: The fat itself: lard, beef tallow, vegetable shortening, or liquid oils — canola, soybean, palm.
story: Shortening means any fat solid at room temperature; the word is about what it does to gluten, keeping strands short so pastry crumbs instead of stretching. Lard was the original. Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès invented margarine from beef tallow in 1869 and the industry moved to hydrogenated vegetable fats after.

Then it moved back. In 2015 the FDA found that artificial trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils were not generally recognised as safe; they were banned from foods sold in the United States from 18 June 2018, with limited extensions to 2020 and 2021. Crisco had already been reformulated in January 2007 to meet the zero-grams-per-serving definition. Denmark had capped industrial trans fats in 2004.

For a donut shop that meant a new fat, a different mouthfeel and, in many kitchens, a new supplier — inside a few years, and not by choice.
how: Filter it, top it up, and change it on a schedule the shop keeps in its head.
today: Fresh fat shows: a pale belt around a filled donut is read in Polish bakeries as evidence the oil had not been used and reused.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): The kettle it sits in.
- kin → paczki (donut): Where fresh oil is read off the donut.
- kin → cake-against-raised (story): How much of it each dough takes up.
sources: s:wp-shortening — Shortening — Wikipedia; s:wp-trans-fat — Trans fat — Wikipedia; s:wp-p-czki — Pączki — Wikipedia; s:wp-lard — Lard — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Allie's Donuts (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/allies-donuts/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/allies-donuts.json
id: allies-donuts
aliases: Allie's Hand-Cut Do-nut Shop
facets: state=RI · status=open · founded=1968 · dough=both
region: New England
what: A shop on Route 2 in North Kingstown, Rhode Island, cutting its donuts by hand since 1968, and the state's landmark of the trade.
story: Frederick Alvin "Allie" Briggs opened Allie's Hand-Cut Do-nut Shop on 1 June 1968 in a former sub sandwich shop, with about forty dollars in hand and a seven-thousand-dollar debt. He was a dairy farmer from Point Judith with ten years of donut experience from a shop in Wakefield. He took $38 on the first day, selling close to a hundred dozen at 39 cents each.

In 1969 his son Ricky was killed by a drunk driver while out delivering donuts for the business alongside his cousin. Briggs nearly closed.
today: Customers drive in from Connecticut and Massachusetts. Saveur listed it among the country's best donut shops in 2008; Thrillist did the same in 2016.
address: 3661 Quaker Lane, North Kingstown, RI
geo: 41.59826, -71.49684 (street)
- kin → dunkin-country (style): The region it competes in, by frying its own.
- kin → donuts-per-capita (story): Rhode Island's density, counted.
- kin → hand-cut (kitchen): What the name claims and the bench does.
sources: s:wp-allie-s-donuts — Allie's Donuts — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

facets: state=CA · status=open · founded=1953 · dough=both
region: The Bay Area
what: A 24-hour counter on Polk Street in San Francisco, busiest after midnight, and two other locations.
story: The shop opened at 1621 Polk Street in 1953 or 1960 — accounts differ — and the original owner is not firmly established, though a city report points to Robert N. Nolt, who ran several businesses on the street. Elinor and Ronald Ahn bought it in 1977. After Elinor died in 2001 it passed to her son and daughter-in-law; Aya Ahn is a co-owner.

Around 2012 the shop introduced the Bob's Donut Challenge: eat a giant donut the size of twelve regular ones in under three minutes, and your name goes on a wall.
today: Two locations in San Francisco and one in Mill Valley.
address: 1621 Polk Street, San Francisco, CA
geo: 37.79182, -122.42128 (street)

## Café du Monde (place)

id: cafe-du-monde
aliases: Cafe du Monde
facets: state=LA · status=open · dough=choux · styles=louisiana-beignet
region: Louisiana
what: An open-air coffee stand on Decatur Street in the French Quarter, selling café au lait cut with chicory and beignets three to an order under powdered sugar.
story: The French brought coffee to the Gulf Coast and the Mississippi around 1700. During the Civil War, New Orleans Creoles stretched short coffee with chicory, which adds a chocolate note to café au lait, and the practice stayed.
today: A landmark, and busy enough that the queue is part of the experience people describe.
address: 800 Decatur Street, New Orleans, LA

## Christy's Donuts (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/christys-donuts/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/christys-donuts.json
id: christys-donuts
aliases: Christy's
facets: state=CA · status=unknown · founded=1977 · dough=both · styles=socal-pink-box
region: Southern California, Cambodian America
what: The La Habra shop Ted Ngoy bought in 1977, and the name he put on every shop he bought after it.
story: Christy's had not done well under its previous owners. It did well under the Ngoys, and they kept the name uniform across the shops they added — by 1979 more than 25 of them, by 1987 thirty-two, and at the peak Ngoy reckoned sixty-five. Ngoy and his wife took the American names Ted and Christy when they became citizens in 1985.

The shops were leased out to relatives and to refugee families Ngoy sponsored, which is how one shop turned into a trade for a community.
today: Shops trading as Christy's Donuts still exist in Southern California. This project has not verified which, if any, descend from the Ngoy shops, and does not claim it.
address: La Habra, CA
geo: 33.93161, -117.94549 (town)
- kin → ted-ngoy (person): Bought it, then made it a name and a system.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The shop the style traces back through.
- kin → the-donut-king (story): The long version.
sources: s:wp-ted-ngoy — Ted Ngoy — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

region: Texas
what: A combination deli, bakery and convenience store on Interstate 35 in West, Texas, selling kolaches, klobasniky and strudel to about 600 people a day.
story: Established in 1983 in a town designated "Home of the official Kolache of the Texas Legislature". A poster in the store counts the year's raw materials in thousands of pounds — over 1,200 pounds of cream cheese, 9,000 pounds of flour.

For a lot of Texans the Czech Stop is where the kolache and the klobasnek stop being a regional food and become a road food: the reason you take I-35 rather than another route.
today: Open around the clock, and busiest when the highway is.

## Leonard's Bakery (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/leonards-bakery/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/leonards-bakery.json
id: leonards-bakery
aliases: Leonard's · Leonard's Malasadas
facets: state=HI · status=open · founded=1952 · dough=yeast · styles=hawaii-malasada
region: Hawaii
what: A Portuguese bakery on Kapahulu Avenue in Honolulu that made the malasada an everyday Hawaiian habit rather than a Carnival one.
story: Margaret and Frank Leonard Rego Sr. opened the bakery in 1952. Rego's mother pushed him to sell malasadas — the holeless Portuguese pastry Portuguese immigrants had brought to the islands at the turn of the twentieth century. Leonard's carried it to a far wider audience than it had before.

A franchise location opened in Japan in 2008.
today: A household name in Hawaii and known well beyond it; the malasada wagons park across the island.
address: 933 Kapahulu Avenue, East Honolulu, HI
geo: 21.28491, -157.81328 (street)

## Randy's Donuts (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/randys-donuts/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/randys-donuts.json
id: randys-donuts
aliases: the big donut · Big Donut Drive-In (original)
facets: state=CA · status=open · founded=1952 · dough=both · styles=socal-pink-box
region: Southern California
what: A drive-in donut counter on West Manchester Boulevard in Inglewood, under a 1950s rooftop donut big enough to be a landmark from the 405. Open around the clock.
story: Russell Wendell, a donut machine salesman, founded a chain of drive-in shops called Big Donut in the late 1940s; the first opened in Westmont in 1951 and the second — this building — in 1952. Wendell moved on to his Pup 'N' Taco chain and sold the Inglewood shop in 1976 to Robert Eskow, who renamed it after his son Randy. Eskow sold it in 1978 to Ron and Larry Weintraub, who kept the name. It changed hands again in 2015.

Four of Wendell's big donuts survive; a fifth became a bagel. At their height there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins carrying 22-foot donuts, and the opening of the first one in December 1949 had clowns, jugglers, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging through the hole.
today: The rooftop donut gets photographed more than anything else in the trade, and the shop now runs additional locations under the same name.
address: 805 West Manchester Boulevard, Inglewood, CA, 90301
geo: 33.96185, -118.37038 (street)
- kin → giant-donut-roof (art): The best-known example of the form.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The regional style it sits inside.
- kin → the-donut-hole (place): The other drive-through landmark, twenty miles east.
- kin → russell-wendell (person): Sold the machines, then built the chain the sign came from.

## Seaside Donuts Bakery (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/seaside-donuts/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/seaside-donuts.json
id: seaside-donuts
aliases: Seaside Bakery · Seaside
facets: state=CA · status=open · founded=1985 · dough=both · styles=socal-pink-box
region: Southern California, Cambodian America
what: A Cambodian-American bakery in Newport Beach, open 24 hours, known for cheap selections and a beachside room that fills up at odd hours.
story: Kong Eap, who came to the United States in the 1970s, opened the bakery in 1985 — one of many Cambodian-American bakeries that opened in the area after Ted Ngoy's shops showed the way. He later handed it to his son, Roger Eap, and went into hospitality. The family also took on Simone's Donuts in Long Beach, which his daughter Melissa Eap runs.

Since the 2020s the shop has drawn heavy attention from Asian-American creators on TikTok, which is a different kind of custom from the college students who kept it going for decades.
today: Still open around the clock.
address: Newport Beach, CA
geo: 33.60869, -117.92897 (town)

## The Donut Hole (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/place/the-donut-hole/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/place/the-donut-hole.json
id: the-donut-hole
aliases: Donut Hole La Puente
facets: state=CA · status=open · founded=1963 · dough=both · styles=socal-pink-box
region: Southern California
what: A drive-through bakery in La Puente shaped like two giant donuts: you drive in through one hole, order, and drive out through the other.
story: The first Donut Hole opened in 1963 in La Puente, though sources disagree — one says the La Puente shop was the second, opened in 1968, and dates the building anywhere from 1947 to 1962. What is settled is that the chain went out of business in 1979, the Lopez family bought the La Puente shop that year and held it until 2003, the Covina branch was remodelled beyond recognition and the rest were demolished. This one is the last working example.

Newlyweds drive through it. Some say for luck; others are less coy about the symbolism. Cars have hit the building more than once.
today: An example of programmatic architecture — a building shaped like what it sells — and among the most photographed donut shops in the country.
address: 15300 Amar Road, La Puente, CA, 91744
geo: 34.03714, -117.95171 (street)
- kin → giant-donut-roof (art): Programmatic architecture, and the one you drive through.
- kin → randys-donuts (place): The other landmark, on a roof rather than around a car.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The style around it.
sources: s:wp-the-donut-hole — The Donut Hole — Wikipedia; s:wp-big-donuts-of-southern-california — Big donuts of Southern California — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

facets: state=WA · status=open · founded=2002 · dough=both
region: The Pacific Northwest
what: A Seattle coffee-and-donut company begun on Capitol Hill, now 17 cafés around Puget Sound.
story: Brothers Mark and Michael Klebeck started Top Pot in February 2002. As of November 2023 it ran 17 cafés, though the donuts are made only at the downtown Seattle and Bellevue kitchens and trucked to the rest.

Its recipes are used for the donuts sold in more than 7,000 Starbucks stores in the United States and Canada, and by the Seattle grocer QFC. They are the official donut at Lumen Field.
today: A shop that makes its own and ships them is a third thing: not a chain kitchen, not a counter with a kettle.

aliases: Voodoo
facets: state=OR · status=open · founded=2003 · dough=yeast
region: The Pacific Northwest
what: A Portland shop built on novelty donuts and a late-night queue, now with locations in several states.
story: Kenneth "Cat Daddy" Pogson and Richard "Tres" Shannon opened the first shop on Southwest Third Avenue in Old Town Portland in May 2003. The logo carries a depiction of Baron Samedi, a figure from Haitian Vodou. Until 2006 the shop opened only at night.

The pink box came from California: Pogson travelled there, saw the boxes, and brought both the box and the slogan home — "Good things come in pink boxes."
today: The pink box now reads as Voodoo's to a lot of people who have never been to a strip-mall shop in Orange County.

## Adolph Levitt (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/person/adolph-levitt/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/person/adolph-levitt.json
id: adolph-levitt
said: Sold the machine, then sold the donut, then sold membership in liking them.
facets: role=inventor · state=NY
region: New York City
what: The Russian refugee who built the first automated donut machine in New York in 1920 and founded the Doughnut Corporation of America.
story: Levitt's machine cut and fried donuts automatically, which turned a bakery job into a production line and made a shop window into a show. He founded the Doughnut Corporation of America, which later started the National Dunking Association, and opened the Mayflower donut shop in Times Square in 1931. At the 1933–34 Chicago World's Fair the machine was billed as the food hit of the Century of Progress.

The farm stands followed: cider-selling orchards took up the machine quickly, and cider donuts became a roadside product.
today: Every depositor over every kettle in every strip-mall shop is downstream of that machine.
- kin → doughnut-corporation-of-america (org): The company he built.
- kin → cake-batter (kitchen): The process his machine automated.
- kin → new-england-cider (style): The trade it created at the roadside.
- kin → national-dunking-association (org): The membership stunt his company ran.
sources: s:wp-doughnut-shop — Doughnut shop — Wikipedia; s:wp-cider-doughnut — Cider doughnut — Wikipedia

said: Worked out what people bought and sold them only that.
facets: role=founder · state=MA
region: New England
what: Opened the Open Kettle in Quincy, Massachusetts in 1948 and renamed it Dunkin' Donuts in 1950.
story: Rosenberg had been selling food to factories and construction sites, and found donuts and coffee were the two things people bought. He built the shop around the pair, introduced a logo in 1953 and the mascot Dunkie in 1954, and started selling franchises in 1955. Johnny Spartos, one of the men running the Quincy shop, talked him into a donut with a handle, made for dunking. His son Bob became chief executive in 1963 at 25, the year the hundredth shop opened.
today: Dunkin' dropped Donuts from its name in 2019 and kept selling them.

## Elizabeth Gregory (person)

said: The one who was actually frying.
facets: role=cook · state=ME
region: New England
what: Hanson Gregory's mother, who by the Smithsonian's account made the deep-fried dough the ring story starts from.
story: She used her son's spice cargo — nutmeg, cinnamon, lemon rind — and put hazelnuts or walnuts in the centre, where the dough might not cook through, and called them doughnuts. That detail is the strongest reading of why a fried cake is named after a nut.
today: The son's version of the story travels; hers explains the word.

## Hanson Gregory (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/person/hanson-gregory/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/person/hanson-gregory.json
id: hanson-gregory
aliases: Captain Gregory
said: Claimed the hole and told it the same way for sixty years.
facets: role=inventor · state=ME
region: New England
what: The New England sailor who said he punched the first hole in a donut in 1847, at sixteen, aboard a lime-trading ship.
story: Gregory said he disliked how greasy twisted donuts were and how raw their centres came out, and punched a hole through the middle with the ship's tin pepper box, later teaching his mother the trick. The Smithsonian's account has his mother, Elizabeth Gregory, frying a deep dough that used his spice cargo — nutmeg, cinnamon, lemon rind — and putting hazelnuts or walnuts in the middle where the dough might not cook through.

The claim is one of several. Michael Krondl suggests the ring came from recipes for a jumble, a ring-shaped cookie; Linda Civitello writes the hole made donuts cook faster. By 1870 a cutter with two concentric circles was in production.
today: Nobody has produced a document that settles it, and the story is repeated as settled anyway.
- kin → hole (term): The claim itself.
- kin → olykoek (term): What came before it.
- kin → elizabeth-gregory (person): The other Gregory in the story.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia

said: Sold donut machines, then built buildings shaped like what they made.
facets: role=founder · state=CA
region: Southern California
what: The machine salesman who founded the Big Do-Nut Drive-In chain and put 22-foot donuts on its roofs.
story: Wendell started the chain in the 1940s; the first shop opened in Westmont in 1951, the second — now Randy's — in 1952. At its height there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins carrying the giant rings. The December 1949 opening of the first big donut came with clowns, jugglers, magicians, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging through the hole.

He sold out in the 1970s and moved to his Pup 'N' Taco chain, which Taco Bell bought in 1984. Four of the big donuts survive; a fifth was converted into a bagel.
today: Municipal construction codes now generally prohibit giant object-shaped buildings, so the surviving ones cannot be replaced.

## Ted Ngoy (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/person/ted-ngoy/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/person/ted-ngoy.json
id: ted-ngoy
aliases: Bun Tek Ngoy · the Donut King
said: He is called the Donut King and the nickname did the work of a business card.
facets: role=founder · state=CA
region: Southern California, Cambodian America
what: The Cambodian refugee who turned one La Habra donut shop into a trade for a community, and lost the fortune it made him.
story: Born in 1941 in Sisophon, near the Thai border, to a Chinese immigrant family; his mother, from Shantou, did not speak Khmer. He was sent to Phnom Penh to study in 1967, married Suganthini Khoeun, worked as a travel agent and tour guide, joined the military in 1970 and, through his brother-in-law Sak Sutsakhan, became a major and military attaché in Thailand. In 1975 he fled the Khmer Rouge with his wife and three children and reached Camp Pendleton through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

He took a janitor's job at Peace Lutheran Church in Tustin and a second job at a gas station, noticed a busy donut shop, and asked how it worked. An affirmative-action hiring programme at Winchell's trained him; he managed a store in Newport Beach. In 1977 he bought Christy's Donuts in La Habra.

By 1979 he had more than 25 shops. He began training relatives and refugees and leasing shops to them — "I sponsored more than 100 families" — living out of a motor home to open new ones. By 1987 there were 32 Christy's; at the peak he reckoned 65. He and his wife took citizenship in 1985 as Ted and Christy, bought a house at Lake Mission Viejo and a second at Big Bear, joined the Republican Party and held fundraisers for George H. W. Bush.

Then the gambling. A 1977 Las Vegas trip introduced him to blackjack; he returned monthly, forged his wife's signature on cheques, borrowed from relatives who leased shops from him and signed shops over when he could not repay. Gamblers Anonymous did not hold: "I cry, everybody cry. After cry, go back gambling."
today: Alice Gu's documentary The Donut King (2020) put the story in front of a national audience. The shops the model produced outlasted the fortune by decades.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The style his system produced.
- kin → christys-donuts (place): The shop he bought first.
- kin → ning-yen (person): Named with him for the pink box.
- kin → winchells (org): Where he learned the trade.
- kin → the-donut-king (story): The long version.
- kin → pink-box (art): The object credited to him.
sources: s:wp-ted-ngoy — Ted Ngoy — Wikipedia; s:wp-the-donut-king — The Donut King — Wikipedia; s:wp-cambodian-americans — Cambodian Americans — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Vernon Rudolph (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/person/vernon-rudolph/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/person/vernon-rudolph.json
id: vernon-rudolph
said: Picked the town because his cigarettes came from there.
facets: role=founder · state=NC
region: The American South
what: Bought a yeast-raised recipe from a New Orleans chef and opened in Winston-Salem in 1937.
story: Rudolph (1915–1973) started at eighteen in his uncle Ishmael Armstrong's general store in Paducah, Kentucky, which sold popular doughnuts; the recipe is believed to trace to an Ohio River barge cook named Joseph LeBeouf, whose light doughnuts contained potatoes. Uncle and nephew moved to Nashville in 1934 and opened The Krispy Kreme Doughnut Company on Gallatin Road.

In 1937 Rudolph opened his own store, choosing Winston-Salem because Camel Cigarettes was headquartered there. He rented 534 South Main Street, in what is now historic Old Salem, sold to grocery stores, and sold hot donuts to people who came by during production between midnight and four in the morning. A local architect, Benny Dinkins, drew the logo. The first store outside the South opened in Akron, Ohio, in 1939.
today: The hot-donut trade he started as a side effect became the company's main idea.

- kin → southern-hot-now (style): The style it built.
- kin → the-2am-shift (kitchen): The schedule the hot donut fell out of.
- kin → hot-now (term): The two words.

what: Adolph Levitt's company: donut machines, mixes, the Mayflower shop in Times Square, and the National Dunking Association.
story: Levitt built the first automated donut machine in New York in 1920 and founded the corporation around it. said: Dropped Donuts from the name in 2019 and kept the donuts.
facets: state=MA · status=open · founded=1948
region: New England, The United States
what: The Quincy, Massachusetts chain that paired coffee and donuts nationally, and the oldest surviving company using the short spelling.
story: Bill Rosenberg opened the Open Kettle in 1948 and renamed it Dunkin' Donuts in May 1950. Franchising started in 1955. Allied Lyons, Baskin-Robbins' holding company, acquired the chain in 1990; its purchase of Mister Donut — founded by Rosenberg's former partner Harry Winokur — and the conversion of those shops drove North American growth the same year. Dawn Donuts went the same way.
today: New England independents compete on frying on site, which is the difference the chain's scale cannot copy shop by shop.

what: The Winston-Salem company built on a bought yeast-raised recipe, a window you can watch the line through, and a lit sign.
story: Vernon Rudolph bought the recipe from a New Orleans chef and rented a building in 1937 in what is now historic Old Salem. Headquarters moved to Charlotte in December 2017, with most operations left in Winston-Salem. A group of franchisees had bought the company back from Beatrice Foods in 1982, ten years after Beatrice acquired it.
today: The early-2010s tunnel-oven shops keep the hot sign lit all day, which is a different promise from the one the sign made in 1937.

facets: state=NY · status=closed
region: New York City, The United States
what: A membership organisation started by the Doughnut Corporation of America in the 1930s to popularise donuts in North America.
story: At its peak it claimed millions of members across more than 300 chapters — actors, athletes, politicians and ordinary members — with Official Dunking Rules treating dunking as a sport: break the donut in half, then swish it rhythmically in coffee, cocoa, tea or milk. It held an annual convention in New York. Presidents included Jimmy Durante, Jack Lemmon, Red Skelton, Joey Bishop and Johnny Carson; Bert Nevins was vice president.

## The Salvation Army doughnut huts (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/org/salvation-army-lassies/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/org/salvation-army-lassies.json
id: salvation-army-lassies
aliases: Donut Girls · Doughnut Lassies
said: "Today I made 22 pies, 300 donuts, 700 cups of coffee."
facets: status=closed
region: The United States
what: The World War I canteens where Salvation Army volunteers fried donuts for American soldiers in France — and the reason there is a National Donut Day.
story: After the United States entered the war in 1917 the Salvation Army sent a fact-finding mission to France, which concluded that enlisted men's needs could be met by canteens — "huts" — serving baked goods and providing writing supplies, stamps and mending. About 250 volunteers went. Baking was hard in abandoned buildings near the front, so two volunteers, Ensign Margaret Sheldon and Adjutant Helen Purviance, turned to donuts. They were an instant hit. Sheldon wrote of one day: "Today I made 22 pies, 300 donuts, 700 cups of coffee."

The women became known to the servicemen as Donut Girls. A misconception ties the donuts to the word doughboy; the term was in use decades earlier.
today: National Donut Day, first Friday in June, began in 1938 as a Chicago Salvation Army fundraiser honouring them.
- kin → national-donut-day (event): The day it produced.
- kin → salvation-army (org): The organisation.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/salvation-army-lassies/salvation-army-lassies-a-red-cross-girls-carrying-fresh-doughnuts-from-an-i-bcbec62.jpg · Public domain · Marjory Collins · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AA_Red_Cross_girls_carrying_fresh_doughnuts_from_an_improvised_kitchen_8d40597v.jpg
sources: s:wp-national-donut-day — National Donut Day — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

facets: state=CA · status=open · founded=1948
region: Southern California, The United States
what: The Temple City, California chain founded by Verne Winchell on 8 October 1948.
story: Under Canadian owner Shato Holdings there were 293 Winchell's locations in the western United States in 1999. By 2004, when Yum Yum Donut Shops bought it, the count was near 200; by 2025 it was about 100 shops in six states, plus Guam and Saipan. Franchises have also operated in Japan, Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia.

An affirmative-action hiring programme at Winchell's trained Ted Ngoy, who managed a store in Newport Beach before buying his own shop — which is how a chain's training programme seeded a generation of independents.
today: The chain shrank while the shops its training produced multiplied.

## Cider donut season (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/event/orchard-season/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/event/orchard-season.json
id: orchard-season
aliases: harvest season · apple picking
said: September to the first hard frost, and then the machine goes quiet.
facets: when=September to November or December · status=seasonal
region: New England, Upstate New York, The Upper Midwest
what: The weeks when orchards and cider mills in the Northeast and Midwest run donut machines for the people who came to pick apples.
story: Cider donut season runs with the apple harvest: September through November or December. Grocery stores put them out as early as August. Food & Wine has pointed out that a year-round cider donut is unlikely to contain fresh-pressed cider.

Donuts were autumn food long before this: the slaughter season produced the surplus fat to fry them in.
today: Leaf-peeping traffic and the donut window are the same business for six weeks a year.

## National Donut Day (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/event/national-donut-day/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/event/national-donut-day.json
id: national-donut-day
aliases: National Doughnut Day
said: Free donut, first Friday in June, and almost nobody knows it is a war memorial.
facets: when=first Friday in June · status=open · founded=1938
region: The United States
what: An American observance on the first Friday of June, with free donuts at many shops.
story: It started in 1938 as a fundraiser for the Chicago Salvation Army: money for people in need during the Depression, and recognition for the Salvation Army Lassies who served donuts to American soldiers in France in the First World War.

About 250 volunteers went to France after the United States entered the war in 1917. Baking in abandoned buildings near the front was difficult, so Ensign Margaret Sheldon and Adjutant Helen Purviance turned to donuts. The men called the women Donut Girls. The idea that this is where the word doughboy comes from is a misconception; the term was in use as early as the Mexican–American War.
today: The giveaway is now a marketing day for chains. The fundraiser it came from is rarely mentioned on the poster.
address: Chicago, IL
geo: 41.8781, -87.6298 (town)
- kin → salvation-army-lassies (org): Whom the day honours.
- kin → salvation-army (org): Who created it.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What gets given away.

provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Paczki Day (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/event/paczki-day/

said: Bakeries post a limit per customer and mean it.
facets: when=Shrove Tuesday · status=open · state=MI
region: Chicago, Detroit
what: The Tuesday before Lent, kept in Polish-American cities — Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit, Windsor — as a day for eating pączki.
story: Pączki are traditionally eaten in Poland on the Thursday before Lent. In Polish communities in the United States the observance moved to Fasnacht Day — the Tuesday — which puts Polish and Pennsylvania Dutch traditions on the same morning.

Hamtramck, Michigan, a city surrounded by Detroit with deep Polish roots, is the best-known American centre of the day.
today: Lines start before dawn; bakeries fry all night ahead of it and sell until the dough runs out.

what: A rectangular raised donut, glazed or iced, sometimes filled.
story: Names for it are regional. Long John runs through the Midwest, Canada and Texas; the Mid-Atlantic and central Canada market it as an éclair, though an éclair is choux and this is yeast; the West Coast says bar, and specifies: maple bar, chocolate bar, filled bar. ## Cruller (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/cruller-word/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/cruller-word.json
id: cruller-word
aliases: kruller · crulla
said: One word, three pastries, and no authority to appeal to.
root: Dutch kruller, from krullen, to curl · first seen: late 18th to early 19th century in the United States, with Pennsylvania Dutch settlers · The Aberdeen crulla is first attested in Edinburgh in 1829 and is thought by the Scottish National Dictionary to copy the American word.
facets: letter=C · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: In North America: either a small loaf- or stick-shaped cake donut, or the choux ring sold as a French cruller.
story: From the Dutch kruller, from krullen, to curl. Pennsylvania Dutch settlers brought it in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. In Europe the shape is a twist or a plaited rectangle pulled through itself; northern Germany calls those Hirschhörner, deer horns, and Scandinavia makes them at Christmas — klejner in Danish, klenäter in Swedish.

Milwaukee's cruller is a glazed loaf-shaped cake donut with a crunchy shell. The Aberdeen crulla is Scottish, first attested in Edinburgh in 1829 and thought to copy the American cruller. Youtiao and mahua both get called Chinese crullers in English.
- kin → french-cruller (donut): The choux one.
- kin → fry-cake (term): The other contested word.
sources: s:wp-cruller — Cruller — Wikipedia

## Donut / doughnut (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/donut-spelling/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/donut-spelling.json
id: donut-spelling
aliases: donut · doughnut
said: Both are correct and people still write in about it.
root: dough + nut, where nut carries the older sense of a small rounded cake or cookie, as in ginger nut · first seen: 1809 (dough-nut, Washington Irving); 1900 (donut, George W. Peck) · John T. Edge attributes the short spelling to the Display Doughnut Machine Corporation in the 1920s, shortened so foreign buyers of its machines could pronounce it.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: Two spellings of the same word. Doughnut is the older form and still dominates in print; donut is American, shorter, and on more signs.
story: The first known printed use of donut is in George W. Peck's Peck's Bad Boy and his Pa, 1900: a character drinks a cup of coffee and eats a donut. John T. Edge writes that the short spelling was invented in the 1920s by the New York-based Display Doughnut Machine Corporation, which cut the word to make it easier for the foreign buyers it hoped would buy its machines. A Los Angeles Times piece of 10 August 1929 has Bailey Millard complaining he cannot swallow "the 'wel-dun donut'".

The two ran side by side for decades: The New York Times used both across a series of "National Donut Week" articles covering the 1939 World's Fair. Dunkin' — Open Kettle in 1948, renamed in 1950 — is the oldest surviving company using the short form. Krispy Kreme, per Oxford, is the notable exception that keeps the long one.
- kin → hole (term): The other thing everyone argues about.
- kin → dunkin (org): The company that carried the short spelling.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Dunking (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/dunking/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/dunking.json
id: dunking
aliases: dunk
said: Break it in half first. There were rules, and a president of them.
root: dunk, from Pennsylvania German dunke, to dip, from Middle High German dunken · The National Dunking Association turned the verb into a membership in the 1930s.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=verb
region: The United States
what: Putting a donut in coffee. For twenty-odd years, an organised pastime with officers.
story: The Doughnut Corporation of America started the National Dunking Association in the 1930s to popularise donuts in North America. At its peak it claimed millions of members across more than 300 chapters, with Official Dunking Rules that treated dunking as a sport and told members to break the donut in half before swishing it rhythmically in coffee, cocoa, tea or milk. There was an annual convention in New York.

Its presidents included Jimmy Durante, Jack Lemmon, Red Skelton, Joey Bishop and Johnny Carson. Bert Nevins was vice president.
- kin → national-dunking-association (org): The organisation.
- kin → the-pot-of-coffee (dish): What you dunk into.
- kin → doughnut-corporation-of-america (org): Who set it up, and why.

## Fry cake (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/fry-cake/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/fry-cake.json
id: fry-cake
aliases: fried cake
said: An old word on an old sign.
root: fried + cake: a cake cooked in fat rather than an oven · In older American usage a doughnut was raised dough and a fried cake was the baking-powder ring — and it was the fried cake that had the hole.
facets: letter=F · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: An older American name for the cake donut, still on some signs and menus.
story: Historically the terms doughnut, cruller and fry cake were used loosely and argued over. In the older usage a doughnut was raised dough, risen and dropped into fat, while crullers and fried cakes were leavened with baking powder — soda, in colonial times — rolled out and cut with a smaller circle taken from the middle. By that usage it was the fried cake that had the hole.

- kin → old-fashioned (donut): The cake ring that kept the old shape.
- kin → cruller-word (term): The other word in the same argument.

## Hot now (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/hot-now/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/hot-now.json
id: hot-now
aliases: hot light · hot doughnuts now
said: Two words, lit up, and the parking lot fills.
root: two words on a lit sign; plain description turned into a signal · The practice predates the sign: Krispy Kreme sold hot donuts during the midnight-to-four production run from 1937.
facets: letter=H · part_of_speech=phrase
region: The United States
what: A lit sign saying donuts are coming out of the fryer at that moment.
story: The practice predates the sign. Vernon Rudolph's Winston-Salem shop ran production from midnight to four in the morning for its wholesale trade and sold hot donuts to individual customers who turned up during it. In the early 2010s Krispy Kreme began building shops with tunnel ovens so the hot sign could stay on all day.

*Inference —* the sign changed what it means. Lit at 3 a.m. it reports a shift; lit at 2 p.m. it reports a piece of equipment.

## Jimmies (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/jimmies/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/jimmies.json
id: jimmies
aliases: sprinkles · hundreds and thousands · nonpareils
said: Boston and Philadelphia say jimmies. Say it in Los Angeles and you get a blank look.
root: uncertain; Just Born Candy Company says it named them after an employee · first seen: 1930, as a cake topping · The Jimmy Fund story postdates the first record by eighteen years.
facets: letter=J · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: The long rod-shaped sprinkles, above all the chocolate ones. The tiny balls are nonpareils.
story: Jimmies is the most popular term for chocolate sprinkles in Boston, Philadelphia and New England. The origin is uncertain; it is first documented in 1930, as a cake topping. The Just Born Candy Company of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, says it invented the product and named them after an employee.

A second story credits Sidney Farber's Jimmy Fund and Brigham's ice cream, which charged a penny extra for chocolate sprinkles to benefit it — but the fund started in 1948, well after the word is first recorded. Nonpareils go back to at least the late eighteenth century, as decoration for pièces montées.
- kin → sprinkle-and-dip (kitchen): What happens with them.
- kin → dunkin-country (style): The region the word belongs to.

## Mom-and-pop (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/mom-and-pop/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/mom-and-pop.json
id: mom-and-pop
aliases: independent · family shop
said: Two people and a lease. The rest is detail.
root: American English for a business run by a married couple or a family · Used here for a shop no company owns, whatever name is on the window.
facets: letter=M · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: A shop owned and worked by the family that runs it, as against a franchise or a company-owned store.
story: The line is blurrier than the phrase suggests. A shop can buy its mix from a national flour company, carry a franchised name on the window, and still be owned outright by the family inside it — every Daylight Donuts store is independently owned and operated, and there are roughly 950 of them. A Spudnut sign may outlive the franchise that sold it. And a single family may hold three shops and run them all itself.

This project counts a shop as independent when no company owns it; the sign on the window is not the test.
- kin → tulsa-mix-shop (style): The shops that complicate it.
- kin → what-is-a-mom-and-pop (story): Where this project draws the line.
- kin → daylight-donuts (org): 950 signs, 950 owners.

## Olykoek (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/olykoek/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/olykoek.json
id: olykoek
aliases: oly koek · oliekoek · oil cake
said: The word survives because Washington Irving wrote it down.
root: Dutch oliekoek, oil cake · first seen: 1809, in Washington Irving's A History of New York · Irving gives it as the Dutch-family name for balls of sweetened dough fried in hog's fat.
facets: letter=O · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: The Dutch fried dough ball that came to New Amsterdam, and the American donut's direct ancestor: sweetened dough fried in fat, with no hole.
story: Dutch settlers brought olykoek — oil cake — to New York in the early eighteenth century. Washington Irving put it in print in his 1809 History of New York: "an enormous dish of balls of sweetened dough, fried in hog's fat, and called dough-nuts, or oly koeks: a delicious kind of cake, at present scarce known in this city, excepting in genuine Dutch families."

The centres of those balls were the problem the ring solved. Elizabeth Gregory, by the Smithsonian's account, put hazelnuts or walnuts in the middle where the dough might not cook through — which is one reading of where the nut in doughnut comes from.
- kin → hole (term): What got punched in it.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): What it became.

## Powdered sugar (term)

region: The United States
what: Sugar ground fine and cut with a little starch to stop it caking. The base of every glaze and the finish on beignets, malasadas and pączki.
story: Confectioner's sugar is graded by fineness — 10X is the finest common grade — and usually carries around 3 percent cornstarch as an anti-caking agent, which is why a glaze made from it sets opaque rather than clear.

## The dozen (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/the-dozen/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/the-dozen.json
id: the-dozen
aliases: a dozen · half dozen · baker's dozen
said: You do not buy one. You buy twelve and eat two in the car.
root: from Old French dozeine, twelve; a baker's dozen is thirteen · The extra one is an old trade practice against selling short weight.
facets: letter=T · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: The unit donuts are sold in, and the reason for the box.
story: *Tradition holds —* the dozen is the trade's unit because a box holds twelve in a single layer without crushing, and because a shop prices twelve below twelve times one to move the tray. A baker's dozen is thirteen, an old trade practice of adding one to be safe against a short weight.

This project has not found a published history of donut dozen pricing in the United States and does not invent one.
- kin → pink-box (art): What a dozen goes into.

- kin → the-price-of-a-dozen (story): What it costs, with dates.

## The hole (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/word/hole/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/term/hole.json
id: hole
aliases: the middle · the ring
said: Sold by the bag, named for the part that is missing.
root: the ordinary English word, applied to the absence and then sold as the piece removed · first seen: ring doughnut claimed by Hanson Gregory for 1847; two-circle cutters in production by 1870 · The thing sold as a donut hole is the dough taken out, not the space left.
facets: letter=T · part_of_speech=noun
region: The United States
what: The absence in the middle of a ring donut, and the argument about who first made one.
story: Hanson Gregory, an American sailor, claimed he invented the ring in 1847 aboard a lime-trading ship at sixteen, punching the middle out with the ship's tin pepper box because he disliked greasy dough and raw centres, and teaching his mother the trick. The Smithsonian has his mother, Elizabeth Gregory, making a deep-fried dough that used his spice cargo — nutmeg, cinnamon, lemon rind.

Other readings compete. Michael Krondl suggests the ring came off recipes calling for a jumble, a ring-shaped cookie already in use. Linda Civitello writes the hole was invented because it let the donut cook faster. By 1870 a two-circle cutter was in production and the question became academic.
- kin → donut-holes (donut): What the missing part is sold as.
- kin → hanson-gregory (person): Who claimed it.
- kin → olykoek (term): What it was before.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Mr. Spudnut and the mascots (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/mr-spudnut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/art/mr-spudnut.json
id: mr-spudnut
aliases: Dunkie · Mr. Spudnut
said: A potato in a chef's hat, in a parade, in 1949.
facets: kind=mascot
region: The United States
what: The cartoon characters donut companies used to sell themselves in the middle of the twentieth century.
story: Spudnut Shops advertised with a cartoon Mr. Spudnut, who turned up in advertisements, in restaurants and in parades, under the slogan "Coast to coast… Alaska to Mexico". Dunkin' Donuts introduced its own mascot, Dunkie, in 1954, a year after its first logo.
today: The mascots are gone and the signs are not, which is why a surviving sign reads as older than it is.
- kin → spudnut (donut): The donut.
- kin → dunkin (org): The other mascot's company.
- kin → neon-donut (art): What outlasted them.

## Neon and the lit sign (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/neon-donut/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/art/neon-donut.json
id: neon-donut
aliases: the hot sign · the neon ring
said: The sign is on before anything else in the building is.
facets: kind=neon
region: The United States
what: Signs that advertise by light: a neon ring, a lit arrow, a plastic panel with DONUTS in red, and the hot sign that says the fryer is going.
story: Krispy Kreme's hot sign has an origin in the schedule rather than in advertising — Vernon Rudolph sold hot donuts to people who turned up during the midnight-to-four production run. Tunnel-oven shops from the early 2010s keep it lit all day.

Spudnut signs are a different kind of survivor: the franchise that sold them reached more than 300 shops in 38 states by 1954 and then vanished, leaving the signs on independent shops.
today: A shop's sign is usually older than its owners, and reads as the shop's real name whatever the paperwork says.
- kin → hot-now (term): The two words.
- kin → spudnut (donut): The vanished franchise on the sign.
- kin → the-sign-outlives-the-owner (story): What that does to a directory.
- kin → giant-donut-roof (art): The daylight version.

## The Anthora cup (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/anthora-cup/

id: anthora-cup
aliases: We Are Happy To Serve You · the Greek cup
said: Blue and white, a Greek key, and a paper cup that became a New York object.
facets: kind=print · state=NY
region: New York City
what: The blue-and-white paper coffee cup with a Greek meander border and the words "We Are Happy To Serve You", designed for New York's Greek-run coffee shops.
story: Greek immigrants ran a large share of the city's coffee shops and diners, and the cup was made for that trade. It has since been treated as a piece of New York design rather than as packaging.
today: The cup appears in films set in New York more reliably than any donut does.

## The donut on the roof (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/giant-donut-roof/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/art/giant-donut-roof.json
id: giant-donut-roof
aliases: big donut · programmatic architecture
said: Twenty-two feet of plaster ring, and it still works.
facets: kind=sign · state=CA
region: Southern California
what: Oversize donuts built on or around Southern California shops to catch drivers: roadside novelty architecture, most of it from the decade after the Second World War.
story: Randy's, beside the 405 near LAX, is the best known of four surviving big donuts built by Russell C. Wendell, who started the Big Do-Nut Drive-In chain in the 1940s. A fifth was converted into a bagel. At one point there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins with 22-foot rings — or thirty feet high, depending on the account. The first opened in December 1949 with clowns, jugglers, magicians, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging from the middle of the hole.

Mrs. Chapman's Angel Food Donuts ran about twenty stores with slightly smaller rings. The Donut Hole in La Puente, a drive-through you enter and leave through the holes of two giant donuts, is described as a distant cousin of the rooftop kind.

One critic called the giant donuts part of a Los Angeles that "bordered on pop art, celebrating the effusiveness of life in the years after World War II" — the same city that gave America an orange juice stand shaped like an orange.
today: Municipal construction codes now generally prohibit oversize object-shaped buildings, so the survivors cannot be replaced, only kept.
- kin → randys-donuts (place): The most photographed one.
- kin → the-donut-hole (place): The one you drive through.
- kin → russell-wendell (person): Who built them.
- kin → neon-donut (art): The other thing on the roofline.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/giant-donut-roof/giant-donut-roof-bellflower-bagels-formerly-a-big-donut-bellflower-lo-14dcf31.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Jengod · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABellflower_Bagels_formerly_a_big_donut_-_Bellflower_Los_Angeles_County_California.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/giant-donut-roof/giant-donut-roof-big-do-nut-drive-in-inglewood-california-lccn2017709532.jpg · Public domain · John Margolies · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABig_Do-Nut_Drive-in%2C_Inglewood%2C_California_LCCN2017709532.tif
sources: s:wp-big-donuts-of-southern-california — Big donuts of Southern California — Wikipedia; s:wp-randy-s-donuts — Randy's Donuts — Wikipedia; s:wp-the-donut-hole — The Donut Hole — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The hand-lettered board (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/hand-lettered-board/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/art/hand-lettered-board.json
id: hand-lettered-board
aliases: the menu board · marker on card
said: Prices in marker, taped over the last prices.
facets: kind=sign
region: The United States
what: The menu written by hand — on card, on a whiteboard, on the glass — and updated by writing over it.
story: *Inference —* a hand-lettered board is the tell of a shop that changes what it sells faster than it can order signage: the egg rolls, the boba, the burrito and the kolache arrive on card taped beneath the printed donut list. This project reads boards this way; it is not a cited finding.

The printed panel above usually carries what the shop has always sold, and the card below carries what is keeping it open.
today: The board is where a directory should look first for what a shop actually does now.
- kin → why-the-egg-rolls (story): What tends to be written on the card.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The shops it is found in.
- kin → the-case (kitchen): What the board describes.

## The pink box (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/art/pink-box/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/art/pink-box.json
id: pink-box
aliases: the box · 1-dozen pink
said: "Good things come in pink boxes" is a slogan somebody else wrote about somebody else's box.
facets: kind=box · state=CA
region: Southern California, The United States
what: The matte pink paperboard box a dozen donuts go into: the most recognisable object in the American trade, and the cheapest.
story: The pink boxes that Southern California shops pack donuts in are attributed to Ted Ngoy and Ning Yen, who were setting other Cambodian families up in shops. Pink stock was cheaper than the glossy white box the trade used.

It travelled. Kenneth Pogson of Voodoo Doughnut adopted the box, and the slogan "Good things come in pink boxes", after a trip to California where he saw the boxes in use.
today: A pink box in a film or on a desk signals donuts without a logo, which is a thing very few products manage.
- kin → ted-ngoy (person): Credited with it.
- kin → ning-yen (person): Credited with it.
- kin → socal-pink-box (style): The style named for it here.
- kin → voodoo-doughnut (place): Carried it north.
- kin → the-dozen (term): What goes inside.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/images/pink-box/pink-box-american-donuts-in-red-box-closeup-49818859171.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · Nenad Stojkovic · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAmerican_donuts_in_red_box_closeup._%2849818859171%29.jpg
sources: s:wp-cambodian-americans — Cambodian Americans — Wikipedia; s:wp-voodoo-doughnut — Voodoo Doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Cake against raised (story)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/story/cake-against-raised/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/story/cake-against-raised.json
id: cake-against-raised
aliases: cake vs yeast · the two doughs
facets: kind=essay
region: The United States
what: Two doughs, one kettle, and an argument every shop settles twice a day. Raised dough is lifted by yeast and takes about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C; cake batter is lifted by baking powder or soda and takes about 90 seconds at 190 to 198 °C. Yeast rings average 38 grams, cake rings 24 to 28. The fat numbers are where the published accounts stop agreeing, and this page lays both out rather than picking one.
- kin → glazed-raised (donut): The raised side.
- kin → cake-donut (donut): The cake side.
- kin → the-fryer (kitchen): Where the difference is settled.
- kin → yeast-raise (kitchen): What costs the time.
- kin → cake-batter (kitchen): What a machine could learn.
- kin → old-fashioned (donut): The cake ring people name.
sources: s:wp-doughnut — Doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-cake-doughnut — Cake doughnut — Wikipedia; s:wp-old-fashioned-doughnut — Old-fashioned doughnut — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## The Donut King (story)

id: the-donut-king
aliases: Ted Ngoy's story
facets: kind=essay
region: Southern California, Cambodian America
what: How one man's shop in La Habra became a trade for a community, and what happened to the man. Ted Ngoy fled the Khmer Rouge in 1975, trained at a chain, bought a shop in 1977, and by the mid-1980s had leased shops to more than a hundred sponsored families. He also gambled it away.

## What counts as a mom-and-pop (story)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/story/what-is-a-mom-and-pop/

aliases: the independence line
facets: kind=essay
region: The United States
what: This site is about independent donut shops, which means it needs a rule for what that is. The rule used here: a shop is independent when no company owns it. The name on the window is not the test, and neither is whose flour is in the mixer.

## Why the egg rolls (story)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/story/why-the-egg-rolls/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/pink-box/api/story/why-the-egg-rolls.json
id: why-the-egg-rolls
aliases: the second menu · donuts and Chinese food
facets: kind=essay
region: The United States
what: A donut shop that also sells egg rolls, or breakfast burritos, or bacon egg and cheese, or kolaches, is not being eccentric. It is doing arithmetic out loud. The people running those shops have said so in print, repeatedly, and this page collects what they said.
